title: Form 10-K Cover
summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2023 Form 10-K identifies the company, Delaware incorporation, headquarters, contact details, and reporting period. It lists registered common and preferred stock, exchange-traded notes, and guarantees, with symbols and exchanges, and notes no Section 12(g) securities. The filing confirms required reports and data files were submitted, classifies JPMorgan as a large accelerated filer, reports auditor attestation of internal controls, and indicates it is not a shell company. It provides market value and share count figures and incorporates portions of its 2024 proxy statement for Part III items.

title: Form 10-K Index
summary: The text is a Form 10-K index covering Parts I–IV: business overview, segments, competition, human capital, regulation, banking and financial topics, risk factors, staff comments, properties, legal proceedings and mine safety; stock matters and reserved items; management’s discussion, market risk, financial statements, accounting changes, controls, other information and foreign inspection disclosures; directors, governance, compensation, ownership, related-party matters, independence, and accounting fees; and exhibits and financial statement schedules.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business.
JPMorgan Chase Overview and Business Segments
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is a Delaware-incorporated global financial services firm with $3.9 trillion in assets and $327.9 billion in equity at year-end 2023, serving consumer, business, institutional, and government clients. The text identifies its principal U.S. bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries and key overseas subsidiaries; explains online access to SEC filings and company information, and its employee and executive ethics codes; and outlines its four reporting segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus Corporate, with references to segment disclosures and the 2023 First Republic acquisition.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase operates in highly competitive markets against a wide range of financial and non-financial firms, including banks, investment and insurance companies, fintechs, and internet-based businesses. Competition centers on product and service quality and variety, execution, innovation, reputation, and price, and varies by client, industry, geography, and whether competition is global, national, or regional. New online-only and non-financial entrants also challenge traditional banking services.

nodes.title: Human Capital
key_items: Firm culture; Attracting and retaining employees; Developing employees
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its human-capital priorities and workforce as of December 31, 2023: 309,926 employees across 65 countries, up 16,203 year over year, with regional and business-line distributions. It reports voluntary employee and leadership diversity data on race/ethnicity, gender, LGBTQ+ status, veteran status, and disability, with definitions and coverage limitations. The text outlines its culture and inclusion principles, recruitment and retention practices, diverse-talent initiatives, fellowships, hybrid work, employee training and leadership development, and compensation philosophy, pay equity reviews, benefits, and 2023 U.S. health and wellness enhancements.

nodes.title: Supervision and regulation
Financial holding company:
key_items: Consolidated supervision; Permissible business activities; Capital and liquidity requirements
Enhanced prudential standards; Resolution and recovery; Orderly liquidation authority; Holding company as a source of strength; Regulation of acquisitions; Ongoing obligations
Holding company as a source of strength
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is subject to extensive U.S. and international oversight: the Federal Reserve supervises the consolidated holding company, while banking, securities, derivatives and foreign subsidiaries face relevant regulators. The text covers restrictions on permissible activities and consequences of failing eligibility or CRA standards; capital, liquidity and leverage rules, including proposed U.S., EU and U.K. Basel III changes; annual supervisory and company stress tests, capital plans and stress-buffer timing; enhanced prudential, governance and risk-management standards; recovery and resolution plans, proposed FDIC plan-rule revisions, and orderly liquidation authority; the parent’s duty to support bank subsidiaries; acquisition approvals and limits; and ongoing DOJ deferred-prosecution and CFTC cooperation obligations.

nodes.title: Subsidiary banks:
key_items: FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory obligations across banking, consumer finance, securities, investment management and derivatives. It covers OCC enforcement and risk-governance standards; FDIC insurance funding, insolvency powers and depositor priority; prompt corrective action, affiliate-transaction and dividend limits; U.S., EU and U.K. supervisory requirements, including EU intermediate parent entities; consumer-protection oversight and proposed fee and interchange rules; broker-dealer conduct and capital regulation; investment-adviser fiduciary duties and proposed DOL retirement-advice rules; and extensive U.S. and international swap-dealer requirements for capital, collateral, clearing, trading, reporting and conduct.

nodes.title: Consumer, Securities and Investment Regulation
nodes.summary: The text describes U.S. consumer regulation, including proposed limits on overdraft fees and debit-card interchange fees and state oversight, and U.K. retail banking and investment regulation, including the Consumer Duty. It outlines broker-dealer oversight and rules governing securities activities and market conduct in the U.S., U.K. and EU. It also covers global asset and wealth management regulation, U.S. adviser and bank fiduciary obligations, ongoing rulemaking, and a proposed DOL fiduciary rule that could affect retirement investment advice and compensation.

nodes.title: Derivatives regulation:
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory obligations across derivatives, data privacy and cybersecurity, anti-money-laundering and sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation, and sustainability. Derivatives rules cover registered swap dealers and a futures commission merchant, with requirements including capital, collateral, clearing, trading, conduct, reporting, and recordkeeping across U.S., EU, U.K., and other jurisdictions. It also describes evolving global data laws; BSA controls and OFAC, EU, U.K., and other sanctions; compliance with the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and U.K. Bribery Act; regulator oversight of incentive compensation; and expanding EU sustainability reporting and due-diligence duties affecting certain entities.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Regulatory and Compliance Obligations
key_items: The Bank Secrecy Act and Economic Sanctions:
nodes.summary: J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is registered with the CFTC as a futures commission merchant and belongs to the National Futures Association. The page describes global data, privacy and cybersecurity regulation; BSA controls, recordkeeping, reporting and customer due diligence, plus U.S., EU, U.K. and other economic sanctions; anti-corruption laws including the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and U.K. Bribery Act; and compensation oversight and standards from U.S. and international regulators, which continue to evolve and may affect compensation programs.

nodes.title: Sustainability:
nodes.summary: U.K. and EU policymakers continue expanding sustainability initiatives and disclosure rules. The EU’s CSRD replaces and broadens certain ESG reporting requirements, with phased implementation beginning for fiscal years in 2024. Agreed in December 2023, the CSDDD requires due diligence on human rights and environmental harms across companies’ operations and certain business relationships, plus company-specific climate transition plans. Both directives affect certain of the Firm’s EU and non-EU entities.

The section describes JPMorgan Chase’s extensive U.S. and international supervision of its holding company and subsidiaries across banking, consumer finance, securities, investment management and derivatives. It covers permissible activities, regulatory approvals, capital, liquidity and leverage rules, stress tests, governance, risk management, recovery and resolution planning, deposit insurance, corrective action, affiliate and dividend limits, and regulatory enforcement. It also addresses consumer and market-conduct rules; broker-dealer, adviser, fiduciary and swap-dealer obligations; derivatives requirements; data privacy and cybersecurity; anti-money-laundering, sanctions and anti-corruption controls; compensation oversight; and expanding EU and U.K. sustainability reporting, due-diligence and climate-plan requirements.

JPMorgan Chase’s business section describes its corporate structure, scale, subsidiaries, ethics resources, reporting segments, and First Republic acquisition. It covers competition from financial, fintech, online, and other firms; workforce size and composition, diversity, culture, hiring, development, hybrid work, compensation, and benefits; and extensive U.S. and international regulation of its activities, including prudential and conduct requirements, capital and liquidity, risk and resolution planning, consumer and market protections, privacy and cybersecurity, financial-crime controls, compensation, and sustainability obligations.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
Summary
Summary (intro)
nodes.summary: The passage cautions that its risk disclosures are not exhaustive and that any risks, alone or together, could materially harm JPMorgan Chase’s business, financial results, condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation. It summarizes regulatory, political, market, credit, liquidity, capital, operational, strategic, conduct, reputation, country, people and legal risks. It then details extensive, evolving global regulation: compliance and supervision can raise costs, reduce revenue, constrain products, activities and liquidity, require asset sales or higher charges, and expose the firm to enforcement, fines, litigation and reputational harm. Regulatory differences may disadvantage large banks versus less-regulated competitors or favor local institutions, potentially costing JPMorgan Chase market share.

nodes.title: Regulatory
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s reputational, country, workforce and legal risks, then details regulatory risks: extensive, evolving oversight may raise costs, constrain business and trigger penalties, while inconsistent rules and less predictable legal systems create competitive, compliance and operational challenges. It discusses enforcement actions and collateral consequences; resolution-plan requirements and possible restructuring; losses that Parent Company debt and equity holders may bear in bankruptcy or receivership; and political and geopolitical uncertainty—including monetary, fiscal, health, climate/ESG, trade and sanctions policies—that can disrupt growth, markets and investor confidence.

nodes.title: Political
nodes.summary: The text explains resolution-plan risks: regulators may impose stricter requirements, restrict growth or operations, or require restructuring or divestitures; in resolution, JPMorgan Chase parent-company debt and equity holders absorb losses, with equity first and unsecured creditors junior to subsidiary, secured, and priority claims. Its preferred single-point-of-entry strategy is not guaranteed, and the FDIC has not formally adopted it. It also describes how political and geopolitical developments, policy shifts, sanctions, trade measures, health emergencies, and climate/ESG actions may disrupt markets, weaken clients and JPMorgan’s finances, liquidity, operations, or credit rating. Conflicting government demands on sensitive industries may trigger restrictions, enforcement, reputational damage, or impaired client and government relationships; similar limits have occurred before.

nodes.title: Market
nodes.summary: The text explains how economic, geopolitical, regulatory and market conditions can harm JPMorgan Chase’s investment, market-making, consumer and wholesale businesses. It covers effects of recessions, inflation, employment, confidence, liquidity, interest rates, credit spreads, asset values, crises and sector-specific shocks; resulting credit losses, lower transaction and asset-management fees, funding and servicing costs, and reduced earnings, liquidity or capital. It details consumer policy impacts; wholesale, commercial real estate and client risks; high- and low-rate consequences; valuation and liquidity uncertainty for financial instruments; and the possibility that hedging, risk management and stress testing fail during extreme events.

nodes.title: Credit
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces credit, operational, legal, reputational, liquidity and market risks from client and counterparty defaults; custodial, CCP or major-market-participant failures; government actions and local legal restrictions; and disputes over derivatives or collateral. Stress and illiquidity can undermine collateral recovery. Concentrated exposures may spread losses across connected industries or regions, while limited diversification and hedging, regulatory reserve requirements, aggressive consumer lending by competitors, and market dislocations that prevent position reductions can increase losses, charge-offs, RWAs, funding costs and capital pressure, or reduce revenue and profitability.

nodes.title: Liquidity
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to JPMorgan Chase from market-participant failures and contagion, declining or disputed collateral values and counterparties’ inability to post collateral, and concentrations of credit and market exposure across related clients, industries and regions. Economic deterioration can trigger losses, reserves, consumer defaults, charge-offs and lower revenues; aggressive competitor lending may worsen these risks. Inability to reduce positions during market disruption can raise risk-weighted assets, harm capital, funding costs and profitability. It also begins a discussion of liquidity constraints, which may result from market disruption, regulatory changes or government and Federal Reserve balance-sheet reduction.

JPMorgan Chase warns that disclosed risks are not exhaustive and may individually or collectively materially harm its business, results, condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation. Risks include evolving and inconsistent regulation, enforcement and resolution requirements; political, geopolitical and policy shifts; economic and market volatility; credit and counterparty defaults; and liquidity constraints. These can raise costs, restrict or restructure operations, disrupt markets, weaken clients, impair collateral and funding, increase losses and capital needs, reduce revenues, and damage relationships or reputation. Concentrations, contagion, competitor behavior, legal uncertainty and ineffective hedging or stress testing may amplify impacts.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase may suffer losses if the value of collateral declines in stressed market conditions.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s credit risk and potential losses may rise during market stress or illiquidity if collateral values decline, collateral cannot be realized or liquidated for enough to cover amounts owed, counterparties cannot post collateral, or valuation disputes prevent the bank from realizing fair value or managing collateral declines.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk.
JPMorgan Chase’s ability to operate its businesses could be impaired if its liquidity is constrained.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces losses from concentrated credit and market exposures linked to related clients, industries, geographies, or business models, where contagion can worsen credit, liquidity, and market risks, require additional reserves, and be difficult to diversify or hedge. Aggressive consumer lending competition may weaken loan standards, increase defaults and losses, and depress revenue or economic conditions. Inability to reduce positions during market disruptions can raise risk-weighted assets, hurt capital, funding costs, and profitability. Liquidity may be constrained by market disruption, regulation, government actions, asset-sale limits, defaults, outflows, deposit losses, or reduced confidence, raising funding costs and limiting access to stable funding. Alternative funding may be costlier or scarce, including when meeting liquidity, resolution-planning, or overseas pre-positioning requirements; poor liquidity management can restrict business funding and investment and harm results.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company and depends on the cash flows of its subsidiaries to make payments on its outstanding securities.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company reliant on subsidiary cash flows. It owns JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and the IHC, which holds most other subsidiaries, other assets, and lends to the Parent Company. The Parent must contribute substantially all securities-issuance proceeds to the IHC. Regulatory, capital, liquidity, and management-imposed limits constrain payments from the Bank and IHC to the Parent. This may impair the Parent’s ability to pay debt interest, equity dividends, redeem or repurchase securities, and meet other obligations, potentially prompting earlier bankruptcy protection or resolution proceedings.

nodes.title: Reductions in JPMorgan Chase’s credit ratings may adversely affect its liquidity and cost of funding.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s risks from credit-rating downgrades, which may limit market access, raise funding and collateral costs, reduce counterparties and investors, hurt profitability, and lower the value of its debt. It describes regulatory capital requirements and potential increases, and how capital shortfalls or stricter rules could constrain buybacks, dividends, capital instruments, and business activity; proposed Basel III changes add uncertainty. It also explains dependence on reliable, secure operational systems and data, risks from outages and third-party disruptions, and resulting customer impacts, including access failures, data theft, duplicate transactions, and service delays.

nodes.title: Maintaining the required level and composition of capital may impact JPMorgan Chase’s ability to support business activities, meet evolving regulatory requirements and distribute capital to shareholders.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from JPMorgan Chase credit-rating downgrades, which could restrict market access and business, raise financing costs and collateral needs, reduce counterparties and investors, and widen credit spreads, lowering the value of its obligations. It explains how capital requirements—including leverage and risk-based rules, GSIB buffers, regulatory actions, balance-sheet and risk changes, and stress-test losses—could constrain buybacks, capital instruments, dividends, and operations; proposed Basel III changes add uncertainty. It also outlines reliance on accurate, secure, maintained operational systems and recurring internal and third-party disruptions that can impair customer access and transactions, expose personal data, duplicate transactions, and delay service.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are dependent on the effectiveness of internal and external operational systems.
nodes.summary: The text describes credit-rating, capital, and operational risks to JPMorgan Chase. Downgrades could restrict market access, raise funding and collateral costs, reduce counterparties and investor participation, widen credit spreads, and lower the value of its obligations. Capital rules and buffers may rise due to regulation, balance-sheet or risk changes, or stress losses; failure to meet requirements could limit buybacks, dividends, capital actions, and business activity. Proposed Basel III changes add uncertainty. Operational systems depend on accurate data, maintenance, security, and third parties; failures, cyberattacks, errors, fraud, or interconnected-system disruptions may harm customers and markets, causing service and settlement problems, losses, higher costs, legal or regulatory consequences, reduced confidence, and reputational damage.

nodes.title: A successful cyber attack affecting JPMorgan Chase could cause significant harm to JPMorgan Chase and its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces frequent, evolving cyberattacks from diverse actors, including malware, denial-of-service, ransomware, geopolitical threats, and third-party service disruptions; past and future breaches could harm the firm and its stakeholders. Risks are difficult to prevent because threats are sophisticated, sources varied, external systems uncontrolled, and intrusions can spread undetected. Exposure may grow through digital expansion, AI, quantum computing, acquisitions, and intercepted mobile communications. Timely improvements to access controls, vulnerability detection, vendor and asset management, resilience, network security, insider-threat safeguards, and acquisition integration are essential. Successful attacks could disrupt operations, steal or damage data, enable fraud or ransom demands, cause losses, legal and regulatory consequences, erode trust, and damage reputation. Investigations and remediation may be prolonged and uncertain, spreading harm, delaying disclosures, and increasing costs.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected if it fails to identify and address operational risks associated with the introduction of or changes to products, services and delivery platforms or the adoption of new technologies.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase may fail to identify new operational risks or implement adequate controls when launching or changing products, services, delivery platforms, or technologies, or acquiring or investing in businesses; risks include greater reliance on third parties. Significant failures could disrupt operations and cause client or counterparty liability, increased compliance, operational, or litigation costs (including regulatory sanctions), reputational damage, liquidity impairment, regulatory intervention, or weakened competitiveness, materially harming its businesses and results.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s business and operations rely on its ability, and the ability of key external parties, to maintain appropriately-staffed workforces, and on the competence, trustworthiness, health and safety of employees.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase depends on adequately staffed, competent, trustworthy, and safe employees, as well as workforces of vendors, custodians, financial-market infrastructures, and potential acquisition targets. Its operations, customer offerings, profitability, and risk management could be harmed by poor business decisions or controls and training, labor shortages, workforce disruptions from health emergencies or extraordinary events, operational failures, theft, fraud, unlawful conduct, human error, or misconduct. Operations may also be impaired if the firm, authorities, or external parties fail to protect workers effectively.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase faces substantial legal and operational risks in the processing and safeguarding of personal information.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces legal, operational, financial, and reputational risks from evolving global privacy and data-protection requirements and the handling of personal information. Compliance, especially across conflicting jurisdictions, can raise costs, constrain products and data use, require management oversight, and make operations less efficient. Inadequate controls by the bank or external parties, unauthorized disclosure or interception, and actual or perceived compliance failures may trigger litigation, investigations, fines, sanctions, operational changes, and loss of clients, customers, or employees. Publicized data incidents are driving stricter regulation, including cross-border transfer, affiliate-sharing, and data-localization restrictions that may increase costs and complexity and hinder product development, delivery, or marketing.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s operations, results and reputation could be harmed by occurrences of extraordinary events beyond its control.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase warns that extraordinary events outside its control—including cyber or physical security incidents, outages, system or data failures, property damage, climate impacts, disasters, health emergencies, accidents, unrest, hostilities and terrorism—could disrupt operations, harm its reputation, cause losses, liabilities, litigation, sanctions and market disruption, and weaken clients’ creditworthiness. Its resiliency program may not fully address single, simultaneous, chronic or geographically concentrated disruptions. The First Republic acquisition may deliver fewer benefits than anticipated, face integration difficulties, employee losses, unexpected costs or losses, and reduced FDIC shared-loss coverage if agreement conditions are breached. Enhanced standards for vendor and service-provider oversight create costs and exposures; failures may harm customers, revenues, operations and reputation or trigger sanctions. Finally, weaknesses in risk management, controls, governance, models, reporting or data quality may cause losses, poor decisions, compliance failures, scrutiny, customer harm and diminished confidence.

nodes.title: First Republic Acquisition and Service Provider Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase’s acquisition of certain assets and liabilities of First Republic Bank may not result in all of the benefits anticipated.
Enhanced regulatory and other standards for the oversight of vendors and other service providers can result in higher costs and other potential exposures.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks that extraordinary events may disrupt market infrastructure, trigger legal or regulatory consequences, damage reputation, and weaken customers’ finances, increasing credit losses. It explains that the First Republic acquisition may fall short of expected benefits due to purchase price, integration costs and timing, asset performance, or other factors; integration disruption, employee departures, unexpected losses, and failure to meet FDIC shared-loss conditions could also cause harm. Enhanced oversight standards for vendors and service providers raise costs, and poor management of these relationships could harm customers, invite sanctions, reduce revenue, increase costs, or damage reputation.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s risk management framework and control environment may not be effective in identifying and mitigating every risk to JPMorgan Chase.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s risk controls may fail to identify or mitigate all risks. Weaknesses in its risk framework, governance, models, reporting, or controls could cause unexpected losses and materially harm financial results, while delaying escalation, worsening decisions, requiring remediation, causing legal or regulatory noncompliance and sanctions, harming customers or reputation, and reducing confidence. Incomplete, inaccurate, or late data can undermine risk management and reporting. Strategies and models rely partly on historical patterns and subjective assumptions that may fail during stress or unforeseen market changes, potentially limiting effectiveness and causing losses.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase could recognize unexpected losses, its capital levels could be reduced and it could face greater regulatory scrutiny if its models, estimations or judgments, including those used in its financial statements, are inadequate or incorrect.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase relies on periodically reviewed models, estimates and judgments—including AI, machine-learning and quantum-computing tools—for risk management, stress testing, financial reporting and regulatory capital calculations. They can fail due to unreliable historical assumptions, forecasting limits, incomplete data, extreme or illiquid markets, technology or data errors, and ineffective reviews. Inaccurate valuations, acquired assets differing from model assumptions, or incorrect credit-loss forecasts may cause unexpected losses and reduced capital. Greater uncertainty may require additional judgment. Regulators must approve certain models used for Basel III risk-weighted assets; rejection could trigger higher capital charges, harm results or constrain business growth, while deficiencies may invite greater scrutiny.

nodes.title: Lapses in controls over disclosure or financial reporting could materially affect JPMorgan Chase’s profitability or reputation.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase warns that ineffective disclosure controls or financial-reporting controls, amid complex and changing regulations, could cause inaccurate reporting, harming results, capital-market access, resources, reputation, investor confidence, or exposing it to litigation and sanctions. Strategic failures—including poor planning, product, geographic, customer, acquisition, investment, capital-allocation, due-diligence, integration, stakeholder, market-response, or resource decisions—could weaken competitiveness, growth, and earnings; costs of disposing of excess facilities may also be material. Intense, evolving competition from banks, financial firms, technology companies, and other nonbanks may hurt results; aggressive nonbank lending could erode bank market share and amplify instability in downturns.

nodes.title: If JPMorgan Chase’s management fails to develop and execute effective business strategies, and to anticipate changes affecting those strategies, JPMorgan Chase’s competitive standing and results could suffer.
nodes.summary: The text warns that control lapses could harm JPMorgan Chase’s operations, capital-market access, finances, reputation and investor confidence, or lead to remediation costs, litigation and sanctions. It explains that ineffective strategy development or execution may weaken competitiveness, growth and earnings. Strategies cover offerings, markets, customers, acquisitions and investments, counterparties, and delivery channels and providers; poor or misinformed choices or failure to adapt to competition, regulation, markets and stakeholder expectations can damage the franchise. Growth also depends on sound planning, resource development, expense control and shareholder returns. Risks include weak plans or products, poor capital allocation or investment oversight, inadequate due diligence or integration, failure to address stakeholder and climate/ESG concerns, slow market response, and insufficient operational, technology, risk, financial or managerial resources. Disposing of excess facilities may also entail material costs.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase faces significant and increasing competition in the rapidly evolving financial services industry.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces intense, growing competition from banks, financial firms, technology companies and other non-banks amid regulatory, technological and economic change. Digital finance, e-commerce, cryptocurrencies and distributed ledgers enable new competitors and may disrupt traditional banking and payments; adapting can raise costs, compliance burdens and reduce income. Competitors’ lending practices may take market share or contribute to industry instability. Competition can pressure prices, reduce market share and revenues if the firm fails to meet customer expectations, and require additional investment or capital for clients.

nodes.title: The effects of climate change could adversely affect JPMorgan Chase’s business and operations, both directly and as a result of impacts on its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: Climate change may harm JPMorgan Chase directly and through its clients across its global operations. Physical risks—acute events and chronic climate shifts—can damage assets, raise insurance costs, disrupt operations and supply chains, and drive migration or unemployment. Transition risks from policy, technology, and consumer changes may devalue assets, increase compliance and energy costs, undermine business models, and damage reputation. Conflicting regional or extraterritorial rules and uncertain data and models may also create risk and inaccurate disclosures or reporting. Employee conduct failures can harm clients and markets, damage reputation, and prompt litigation or regulatory action.

nodes.title: Conduct failure by JPMorgan Chase employees can harm clients and customers, impact market integrity, damage JPMorgan Chase’s reputation and trigger litigation and regulatory action.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from financial technology competition and disruption, including new digital services, cryptocurrencies and distributed ledgers, which may require investment, increase compliance costs, reduce revenue, pressure prices and market share, and require additional capital. Climate change poses physical and low-carbon-transition risks to JPMorgan Chase and its clients, affecting assets, insurance, operations, energy costs, business models, reputation and creditworthiness; inconsistent policies and uncertain data and models may also cause inaccurate reporting. Employee misconduct can harm customers, markets and reputation and trigger litigation, investigations, sanctions, losses, higher costs, regulatory restrictions, oversight and customer losses. Examples include mis-selling, trading abuses, fraud, improper transactions, fiduciary breaches, collusion, unauthorized communications, discrimination, poor risk management and misappropriation; risks may be heightened in acquired businesses.

The section outlines risks from concentrated credit and market exposures, aggressive lending, constrained liquidity and funding, rating downgrades, and regulatory capital requirements that may limit operations and shareholder distributions. It covers the parent company’s dependence on subsidiary cash flows; operational, cyber, technology, third-party, workforce, privacy, and extraordinary-event risks; First Republic acquisition and service-provider risks; and weaknesses in risk management, models, controls, reporting, and strategic execution. It also addresses competition, climate impacts, and employee misconduct, all of which may cause losses, regulatory or legal consequences, reputational harm, and reduced business performance.

nodes.title: Reputation Damage to JPMorgan Chase’s reputation could harm its businesses.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s risks from reputational damage, including misconduct, security and privacy failures, ESG and regulatory issues, adverse publicity, activism, public-policy criticism, industry behavior, and conflicts of interest or fiduciary failures, with potential business, financial, and regulatory consequences. It describes risks from international conflict and volatile country conditions; employee recruitment, retention, hybrid work, and immigration policies; and litigation, investigations, and enforcement. It also notes no unresolved staff comments, refers cybersecurity discussion elsewhere, provides headquarters and excess-property information, points to material legal proceedings, states mine-safety disclosures are not applicable, and lists facilities by region and U.S. retail branches.

JPMorgan Chase describes risks that could materially harm its business, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation, including regulatory and political change, economic and market volatility, credit, collateral, counterparty, liquidity and funding risks, concentrated exposures, and contagion. It covers operational, cyber, technology, third-party, workforce, privacy, climate, acquisition, risk-management, model, control and execution weaknesses; competition, misconduct, conflicts, reputational damage, international instability, litigation and enforcement; and effects on costs, losses, revenues, operations and distributions. The section also addresses facilities and branches, legal proceedings, cybersecurity references, staff comments and mine-safety disclosures.

nodes.title: Staff Comments, Cybersecurity, Properties, and Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: There are no unresolved staff comments. Cybersecurity risks are discussed in the Operational Risk Management section of Management’s discussion and analysis. JPMorgan Chase’s headquarters is its owned 47-story building at 383 Madison Avenue; demolition of its former 270 Park Avenue headquarters was completed in 2021, and a new headquarters is under construction there. Excess properties may be difficult to dispose of and could incur material costs; occupancy expense is discussed in the Consolidated Results of Operations. Material legal proceedings are described in Note 30.

nodes.title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures.
key_items: Parts I and II; Item 1C. Cybersecurity.; Item 2. Properties.
nodes.summary: The text states that mine safety disclosures are not applicable. It lists the Firm’s 72.3 million square feet of owned or leased facilities worldwide as of December 31, 2023, including U.S. locations, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Canada, and notes 4,897 retail branches across 48 states and Washington, D.C.; facilities serve all business segments and corporate purposes, with space needs continually reviewed. It describes common-stock listing, performance and dividend information references, 204,357 holders of record, and employee-plan securities references. It reports 2023 share repurchases by quarter, including 69.5 million shares, average price of $142.31, $9.9 billion aggregate cost, and $19.735 billion remaining under the $30 billion authorization, noting the 1% excise tax. Items 6 is reserved; Items 7 and 7A direct readers to the MD&A and its market-risk disclosures, respectively.

summary: Part I covers JPMorgan Chase’s business, corporate structure, scale, workforce, competition, acquisition activity and extensive regulation; risks that could affect its finances, operations, reputation and distributions; and related disclosures on staff comments, cybersecurity, facilities, branches and legal proceedings. It also reports mine-safety inapplicability, facility and branch counts, stock listing and holder information, share repurchases and authorization, and directs readers to management’s discussion and market-risk disclosures.

Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations.

It describes the $30 billion share repurchase authorization and reports 2023 repurchase shares, average prices, purchase amounts, and remaining authorization, noting the 1% excise tax and excluding tax and commissions. Item 6 is reserved. Item 7 directs readers to the MD&A and related consolidated financial statements and notes.

nodes.title: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk.
key_items: Repurchases under the common share repurchase program
nodes.summary: Item 7A refers readers to the market risk discussion on pages 135–143. Item 8 identifies the consolidated financial statements, PwC’s February 16, 2024 report, and the glossary. Item 9 reports no accounting or financial disclosure disagreements. Item 9A describes the COSO 2013 framework assessment of financial-reporting controls, management’s evaluation and conclusion that disclosure controls were effective, and related certifications. It notes inherent control limitations and potential future deficiencies. Controls for assets and liabilities acquired from First Republic Bank were included in the evaluation; no other material control changes occurred in the final quarter of 2023.

nodes.title: Financial Statements and Accountant Disclosures
key_items: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.
Item 9. Changes in and Disagreements With Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure.
nodes.summary: The consolidated financial statements, notes, and February 16, 2024 report of independent auditor PwC (PCAOB ID 238) appear on pages 163–309; the glossary of terms and acronyms appears on pages 315–321. There were no changes in or disagreements with accountants regarding accounting or financial disclosure.

nodes.title: Item 9A. Controls and Procedures.
key_items: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.

nodes.title: Consolidated Results of Operations
Revenue
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase compares 2023 and 2022 operating results, directing readers to prior-year comparisons, segment discussions, and critical accounting estimates. It reports revenue categories and explains changes: investment banking fees fell; lending and deposit fees and asset management fees rose; principal transactions increased despite lower Markets net interest income and funding costs; commissions, card income, and other income rose; securities losses increased; and mortgage income is discussed by reference. Other income reflects First Republic’s bargain gain and other gains, offset by lower lease income and investment losses. Net interest income rose on higher rates, First Republic, and Card balances, partly offset by Markets income and deposits; average asset balances, yields, and non-GAAP net yield measures are also provided.

nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 provisions for credit losses by consumer, card, wholesale and securities categories. It also presents noninterest expenses and categories for 2021–2023: 2023 increases in compensation reflected staffing, wage inflation, First Republic and business activity; noncompensation rose with FDIC assessments, legal costs, First Republic, investment and other expenses, partly offset by lower auto-lease depreciation. Finally, income and tax data show a higher 2023 effective tax rate, attributed to income and tax-mix changes, lower audit-settlement benefits and stock awards, partly offset by First Republic-related tax and regulatory benefits.

nodes.title: Consolidated Balance Sheets and Cash Flows Analysis
nodes.summary: Analyzes JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 balance-sheet changes versus 2022 and cash flows for 2023 and 2022, with references to related accounting estimates, notes, risk sections, and segment disclosures. Assets rose overall: cash increased; resale agreements and investment securities declined; securities borrowed, trading assets, loans, allowances, premises, intangibles, and goodwill increased; receivables and other assets fell. Changes reflect market activity, maturities, loan growth, acquisitions (especially First Republic and CIFM), credit-loss estimates, and investment and collateral shifts. Liabilities and equity also rose: deposits, repos, trading liabilities, VIE interests, and long-term debt increased, while other liabilities declined; drivers included client activity, funding needs, acquisitions, and the FDIC assessment. Cash-flow analysis covers operating, investing, and financing activities, their main 2023 and 2022 sources and uses, and the Firm’s assessment that liquidity is sufficient.

nodes.title: Explanation and Reconciliation of the Firm's Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures
Non-GAAP financial measures
nodes.summary: The Firm reports U.S. GAAP results for consistent year-to-year and peer comparisons, while management also uses non-GAAP managed-basis results and other non-GAAP measures to evaluate performance, trends, and business segments. Managed results reclassify revenue to a fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) basis, making taxable and tax-exempt revenue comparable; related tax effects are recorded in tax expense, with no impact on net income. Measures may differ from similarly named measures at other companies. A reconciliation table compares reported and managed results for 2021–2023, including revenue, expenses, pre-provision profit, credit-loss provisions, pretax income, taxes, net income, and overhead ratios; FTE adjustments are predominantly in CIB, CB, and Corporate.

nodes.title: TCE, ROTCE and TBVPS
nodes.summary: Defines TCE, ROTCE, and TBVPS as non-GAAP measures used by the Firm, investors, and analysts to assess equity use: TCE is common equity less goodwill and non-MSR intangible assets, net of related deferred tax liabilities; ROTCE is net income applicable to common equity divided by average TCE; TBVPS is period-end TCE per common share. A reconciliation shows period-end and annual average common equity, goodwill, other intangibles, qualifying deferred tax liabilities, and resulting TCE, alongside ROTCE and TBVPS where applicable. Qualifying deferred tax liabilities relate to tax-deductible goodwill and intangibles from nontaxable transactions.

nodes.title: Business Segment Risk, Costs, and Capital Allocation
key_items: Debt expense and preferred stock dividend allocation
nodes.summary: Foreign exchange risk on certain revenues and expenses is transferred from business units to Treasury and CIO, which manage it centrally and report its impact. Through funds transfer pricing, nearly all unsecured long-term debt credit-spread costs and preferred stock dividends are allocated to reportable segments, with the remainder retained in Corporate; allocation reflects regulatory capital requirements and funding needs. Debt costs reduce segment net interest income, while dividends reduce net income applicable to common equity. Segment equity allocation uses Basel III standardized risk-weighted assets, the GSIB surcharge, and severe-stress capital simulations; methods are reassessed at least annually, potentially changing allocations.

nodes.title: Firmwide Risk Management
Risk governance framework
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its goal of balancing client and investor service with Firm safety through shared risk responsibility, LOB ownership, governance, and compensation oversight. Its framework considers risk drivers, four risk types—strategic, credit and investment, market, and operational—and quantitative and qualitative impacts. Independent Risk Management, led by the CRO under Board Risk Committee oversight, sets and oversees governance. The three defense lines are business units, IRM, and Internal Audit; other functions also support controls. LOBs and Corporate identify and manage risks, while IRM challenges and consolidates them. Senior management and the Board Risk Committee set and monitor quantitative and qualitative risk appetite.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight structure
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Firm’s risk governance and escalation structure, including the Operating Committee’s role in referring matters and informing the Board. It describes Board oversight and the responsibilities of its independent committees: Board Risk, Audit, Compensation & Management Development, Public Responsibility, and Corporate Governance & Nominating. It also summarizes management risk committees: Firmwide Risk and Control, business and regional risk/control committees, ALCO, and the Valuation Governance Forum. Finally, it lists risk oversight functions covered in subsequent sections, spanning strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, credit, investment, market, country, climate, operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and model-estimation risks.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight functions
nodes.summary: The text outlines Board committee responsibilities: compensation and benefits, executive performance, awards, succession, culture and conduct; public responsibility issues and guidance; and Board governance, nominations and evaluation. It describes management risk committees overseeing firmwide risk, compliance and operational controls, line-of-business and regional risks, asset-liability management, and valuation. It then introduces the Firm’s risk governance and oversight functions, noting that activities can involve multiple risk drivers and types, and lists coverage areas from strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, credit, investment, market, country and climate risks to operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and model-estimation risks.

nodes.title: Strategic Risk Management
Management and oversight
nodes.summary: Strategic risk covers threats to financial performance or reputation from flawed plans or inadequate responses to change. The Operating Committee, business leaders, IRM and Board oversee these risks through governance, risk identification, initiative assessments and periodic strategic planning, which informs the budget and incorporates risk appetite, capital, earnings and balance-sheet objectives. Capital risk is insufficient capital under normal or stressed conditions. Independent Capital Risk Management oversees metrics, limits, breaches, management activities and regulatory compliance; Treasury and CIO manage capital to support investment, resilience, distributions, subsidiaries and resolution needs. Governance involves capital and asset-liability committees and the Board Risk Committee. Annual Federal Reserve CCAR reviews capital plans, stress resilience and distributions; the 2023 SCB was 2.9%, and the standardized CET1 requirement was 11.4%.

nodes.title: Capital Risk Management
Capital planning and stress testing
nodes.summary: The text describes the Firm’s capital risk philosophy and strategy: maintaining a strong, resilient balance sheet and sufficient capital for business needs, risks, investment, and stressed conditions. An independent Capital Risk Management function oversees risk measures, limits, breaches, capital-management assessments, and regulatory compliance. Treasury and CIO manage capital to meet business, subsidiary-support, regulatory, distribution, and resolution needs through internal requirements, governance, flexibility, monitoring, and escalation. Governance involves management committees and Board review. Annual Federal Reserve CCAR assesses capital adequacy, stress planning, and distributions; the Firm’s SCB is 2.9% through September 30, 2024, and its year-end 2023 standardized CET1 requirement was 11.4%. Annual ICAAP integrates stress testing and planning and is reviewed by the Audit Committee; scenarios cover macroeconomic, market, and operational risks, supplemented by tailored stresses and sensitivity analyses.

nodes.title: Contingency Capital Plan
nodes.summary: The Contingency Capital Plan sets the Firm’s capital management framework and principles for normal and stressed conditions. It explains how the Firm sets targeted capital levels, meets minimum requirements, monitors planned distributions, and identifies contingency actions to take or consider at different levels of capital depletion during stress.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
Basel III Overview
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve and OCC set capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase and its bank, generally aligned with Basel standards. Basel III uses risk-weighted assets (RWA) under Standardized and Advanced approaches, with adequacy assessed against the more restrictive applicable ratios; the approaches differ mainly in credit-risk calculations, and Advanced also includes operational risk. A 2023 U.S. Basel III proposal would replace Advanced with an expanded approach, apply the stress capital buffer to both approaches, and substantially increase requirements. The Firm estimates roughly 30% higher RWA and 25% more required CET1 capital after transition, plans to build capital, and says its prior 13.5% CET1 target is no longer meaningful. It may adjust RWA using management judgment. At year-end 2023, Advanced constrained total capital, while Standardized constrained CET1 and Tier 1; the SLR was most binding in fourth-quarter 2023, but a 2024 GSIB surcharge increase is expected to make risk-based ratios more binding again.

nodes.title: Other Key Regulatory Developments GSIB Surcharge
nodes.summary: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve proposed changes to the GSIB surcharge calculation. The Firm would assess its surcharge annually using the average of quarterly calculations, with daily averaging for certain measures; surcharge increments would decrease from 50 to 10 basis points, alongside technical changes to Method 2. The amendments would revise risk-based capital requirements for the Firm and other U.S. GSIBs and take effect two calendar quarters after the final rule is adopted. Further information is cited on pages 94–95.

nodes.title: TLAC and Eligible LTD Requirements
nodes.summary: In August 2023, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC proposed extending TLAC eligible long-term debt and clean holding company requirements to non-GSIB banks with at least $100 billion in consolidated assets. The proposal would also limit how much GSIB debt with less than two years remaining maturity counts toward TLAC and extend the LTD capital deduction framework to covered non-GSIBs.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s Basel III risk-based capital requirements: a 4.5% minimum CET1 ratio plus buffers, including the GSIB surcharge, countercyclical buffer and fixed or variable conservation buffer. It explains the two annual GSIB surcharge methods, reports 2022–2024 rates, and notes the effective 4.5% surcharge from January 2024, a 0% U.S. countercyclical buffer, and possible distribution and bonus limits for shortfalls. It also describes TLAC and eligible debt requirements, the 3% minimum SLR plus a 2% buffer and related penalties, and separate well-capitalized requirements for the Firm and its bank subsidiary, with references to further disclosures.

nodes.title: Capital Buffers, TLAC, and Leverage Requirements
key_items: Leverage-based Capital Regulatory Requirements Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.summary: The page reports the Firm’s 2022–2024 GSIB surcharges and explains their effective dates, the 0% U.S. countercyclical buffer and how it may be raised, and distribution and bonus restrictions for failing capital requirements. It notes Federal Reserve TLAC and eligible long-term debt minimums for U.S. GSIB holding companies. It defines the supplementary leverage ratio (SLR), its 3% minimum and the Firm’s additional 2% buffer, describes total leverage exposure, and outlines consequences of falling below the SLR requirement.

nodes.title: Other regulatory capital
nodes.summary: The Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must meet minimum capital and leverage ratios to qualify as “well-capitalized” under Federal Reserve regulations and FDIC Prompt Corrective Action requirements, in addition to Basel III capital ratios. Note 27 and the Firm’s website Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures provide further information on capital ratios, regulatory standards, and current capital measures.

Covers Basel III risk-weighted capital frameworks and the proposed U.S. changes, including estimated increases in RWA and CET1 needs, the Firm’s capital plans, and which ratios are most binding. It describes proposed GSIB surcharge revisions and TLAC/eligible long-term debt rules, current risk-based capital buffers and surcharge rates, leverage and SLR requirements and consequences of shortfalls, and separate well-capitalized standards for the Firm and its bank subsidiary, with references to further disclosures.

nodes.title: Selected capital and RWA data
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s December 2023 and 2022 Basel III Standardized and Advanced risk-based capital metrics, ratio requirements, and leverage metrics, with references to related bank disclosures and notes. It explains First Republic exposure treatment under transition rules, CECL transition effects, applicable minimum ratios and buffers, and the adjusted-average-assets calculation used for leverage ratios.

nodes.title: Capital components
nodes.summary: The table reconciles JPMorgan Chase’s stockholders’ equity to Basel III CET1, Tier 1 and total capital under Standardized and Advanced approaches at December 31, 2023 and 2022, listing equity deductions and additions, qualifying Tier 2 instruments and credit-loss allowances, and resulting capital amounts. Notes explain deferred tax liabilities, other CET1 adjustments (cash-flow hedges, DVA and CECL transition benefits), goodwill deductions, allowance eligibility and limits, the Advanced Tier 2 reserve adjustment, and a First Republic-related allowance included under transition rules.

nodes.title: Capital rollforward
nodes.summary: The text presents 2023 Basel III CET1, Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital rollforwards, including income, dividends, share repurchases, AOCI and other adjustments, ending with Standardized and Advanced total capital. It reports Standardized and Advanced RWA changes by credit, market and operational risk, explains drivers and disclosures, and gives supplementary leverage ratio components and ratios for 2023 and 2022. It also describes capital allocation methodology, annual reassessment and line-of-business equity allocations for 2022–2024, including First Republic impacts and performance measures.

nodes.title: Line of business equity
nodes.summary: The discussion details 2023 Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA rollforwards by credit, market and operational risk, explaining model/data and portfolio drivers, off-balance-sheet RWA, First Republic treatment, and referring readers to Pillar 3 disclosures. It reports year-end supplementary leverage ratio components and SLRs of 6.1% in 2023 versus 5.6% in 2022, with calculation notes. It also describes annual line-of-business capital allocation methodology, stress considerations and 2024 allocation changes, lists allocated equity by segment for 2022–2024, and explains peer/regulatory factors and ROE performance measures.

nodes.title: Capital actions
key_items: Common stock dividends; Common stock; Preferred stock
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s capital actions. Common dividends are set within its capital governance framework, currently $1.05 quarterly per share subject to Board approval; payout ratios were 25% in 2023, 33% in 2022, and 25% in 2021, with restrictions detailed in cited notes. A $30 billion repurchase authorization took effect May 2022; repurchases were 69.5 million shares ($9.898 billion) in 2023, 23.1 million ($3.122 billion) in 2022, and 119.7 million ($18.448 billion) in 2021. The text notes the 2023 excise tax, 2022 suspension and 2023 resumption, and 2021 regulatory limits. Management controls timing and amounts based on market, legal, capital, regulatory, and investment factors; there are no price targets or timetable, and purchases may be suspended or made through market, private, or Rule 10b5-1 transactions. Preferred dividends were $1.5 billion in 2023 and $1.6 billion in each prior year; further information on preferred stock and subordinated debt is referenced.

nodes.title: Other capital requirements
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve requires U.S. GSIB holding companies, including the Firm, to meet minimum external total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) and eligible long-term debt (LTD) levels. Falling below requirements plus buffers restricts capital distributions and certain executive bonuses. A table reports 2023 and 2022 eligible TLAC and LTD, their percentages of risk-weighted assets (RWA) and total leverage exposure, regulatory requirements, and surpluses or shortfalls, applying CECL transition provisions. From January 1, 2023, TLAC-to-RWA and LTD-to-RWA requirements rose 50 basis points to 23% and 10% because of higher GSIB requirements. The text directs readers to related capital, liquidity, and resolution-risk disclosures.

nodes.title: U.S. broker-dealer regulatory capital
nodes.summary: J.P. Morgan Securities, JPMorgan Chase’s principal U.S. broker-dealer and a registered futures commission merchant, is subject to capital requirements from the SEC, CFTC, FINRA, and NFA and uses the Net Capital Rule’s alternative method. At December 31, 2023, its net capital was $27.865 billion versus a $5.346 billion minimum. As a registered security-based swap and swap dealer, it must maintain tentative net capital above $5 billion and notify regulators if it falls below $6 billion; it exceeded both thresholds at year-end.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. subsidiary regulatory capital
nodes.summary: The text reports that J.P. Morgan Securities plc and JPMorgan SE are regulated non-U.S. subsidiaries subject to Basel III capital rules and MREL; both met MREL and exceeded applicable capital and leverage minimums at year-end 2023. It then describes the Firm’s liquidity risk definition, independent oversight by Liquidity Risk Management, Treasury and CIO’s liquidity-management responsibilities and centralized global approach, governance committees and Board oversight, and internal stress testing across adverse funding, outflow, downgrade, collateral, jurisdictional and time-horizon scenarios. Stress-test results inform funding plans; the Parent Company and intermediate holding company provide funding, while liquidity is maintained across entities to meet tolerances and requirements.

Describes the Firm’s capital strategy, governance, planning, stress testing, contingency actions, and regulatory compliance. Covers Basel III capital and leverage frameworks, requirements and proposed changes; capital ratios, components, rollforwards, RWA, SLR, and line-of-business equity allocation; dividends, share repurchases, preferred capital, TLAC and eligible debt; and U.S. and non-U.S. subsidiary capital requirements. It also outlines liquidity-risk oversight, governance, stress testing, funding plans, and management across entities.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Management
Internal stress testing
nodes.summary: Defines liquidity risk as inability to meet cash or collateral needs or maintain appropriate funding. Describes independent Liquidity Risk Management oversight, including metrics, limits, breach monitoring, process reviews, stress testing, reporting, and assumption approval. Treasury and CIO manage liquidity to support obligations and client needs, optimize funding, comply with regulations, and set liquidity-sensitive transfer pricing. A centralized global approach monitors exposures, transfer constraints, and surplus liquidity. Governance involves ALCOs, treasury and risk committees, and Board Risk Committee review. Regular and event-driven stress tests model funding access, outflows, downgrades, collateral haircuts, and transfer restrictions; results inform funding plans. Parent, IHC, and subsidiaries maintain liquidity to meet requirements and withstand funding disruption.

nodes.title: Contingency funding plan
nodes.summary:
Contingency funding plan
The Firm’s Contingency Funding Plan (“CFP”) sets out the strategies for addressing and managing liquidity resource needs during a liquidity stress event and incorporates liquidity risk limits, indicators and risk appetite tolerances. The CFP also identifies the alternative contingent funding and liquidity resources available to the Firm and its legal entities in a period of stress.

nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.summary: The LCR rule requires the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to maintain eligible, unencumbered HQLA sufficient for stressed 30-day net cash outflows, with a 100% minimum LCR; nontransferable excess bank HQLA is excluded from the Firm’s reported amount. The table reports average LCR and HQLA measures for Q4 2023, Q3 2023, and Q4 2022: the Firm’s LCRs were 113%, 112%, and 112%, and the bank’s were 129%, 123%, and 151%. HQLA includes central-bank cash and eligible securities, mainly Treasuries, agency mortgage-backed securities, and sovereign bonds, subject to regulatory haircuts. The bank’s LCR rose quarter over quarter due to CIB market activity, partly offset by loan growth, and fell year over year due to lower cash and HQLA, deposit declines, loan growth, First Republic, and lower securities values, partly offset by CIB activity. Federal Reserve actions have reduced deposits and, alongside business activity and other factors, may cause LCR fluctuations; the text directs readers to related notes and LCR disclosures.

nodes.title: Liquidity sources
nodes.summary: The Firm had unencumbered marketable securities, including excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that cannot be transferred to non-bank affiliates, valued at $649 billion in 2023 versus $694 billion in 2022. The decline reflected lower excess eligible HQLA, partly offset by higher unencumbered AFS securities; realizable liquidity depends on market conditions. Available cash and securities totaled about $1.4 trillion in both years, comprising eligible HQLA of $798.0 billion in 2023 and $735.5 billion in 2022 (before regulatory haircuts) plus those securities. FHLB and Federal Reserve discount-window borrowing capacity backed by pledged collateral was $340 billion versus $323 billion, increasing mainly due to more wholesale loans pledged. This excludes certain already-counted or other pledged assets, and the Firm does not consider central-bank borrowing a primary liquidity source.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.summary: The NSFR measures whether large banking organizations have enough available stable funding to cover required funding over a one-year horizon. For the three months ended December 31, 2023, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. met the 100% minimum requirement, based on the Firm’s interpretation of the final rule. Further information is available in the Firm’s U.S. NSFR Disclosure report for December 31 and September 30, 2023.

nodes.title: Funding
Sources of funds
nodes.summary: Management believes secured and unsecured funding capacity is sufficient for the Firm’s on- and off-balance-sheet, short- and long-term obligations. Funding comes from diverse sources: stable deposits, capital-market secured and unsecured borrowing, and stockholders’ equity. Bank subsidiaries rely mainly on deposits, with access to secured borrowings, long-term unsecured debt, and IHC borrowing; non-bank subsidiaries rely mainly on long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowing, including securities lending and repurchase agreements. Treasury and CIO invest excess funds in securities, cash, or other short-term liquid investments according to interest-rate and liquidity risks. Note 28 provides further information on off-balance-sheet obligations.

nodes.title: Deposits

It details factors behind changes in average and year-end deposits, including First Republic, customer spending, rate-driven investment shifts, deposit attrition, structured-note issuance, and international initiatives. It also provides uninsured deposit estimates and time-deposit maturities, loan-to-deposit metrics, U.S. and non-U.S. deposit balances and average rates for 2021–2023, and references related disclosures and the following section on non-deposit funding.

nodes.title: Sources of funds (excluding deposits)
nodes.summary: The table reports funding sources excluding deposits, in millions, for year-end 2023 and 2022 and annual averages for both years. It details short- and long-term unsecured and secured funding, including borrowings, repurchase agreements, notes, securitizations, FHLB advances, equity, and totals. Notes explain classifications and consolidated-entity treatment, TLAC-eligible and secured structured notes, the First Republic acquisition Purchase Money Note, equity references, and $500 million of short-term and $23.2 billion of long-term First Republic-related FHLB advances at 2023 year-end.

nodes.title: Short-term funding
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s short-term secured funding, mainly securities lending and repurchase agreements backed largely by high-quality government and agency securities; year-end repo balances rose in 2023 due to less netting, while balances fluctuate with client activity, financing needs, liability management, and market factors. Short-term unsecured funding comprises commercial paper and other borrowings; 2023 period-end commercial paper rose, average balances fell, and average secured other borrowings declined, mainly reflecting liquidity management and lower Markets financing. Long-term funding supports stable liquidity and is planned around client activity, liquidity, regulation (including TLAC), diversification, market access, and cost. The Parent Company issues most long-term debt and passes proceeds to the IHC, which does not issue external debt; structured notes rose due to Markets client demand and fair-value increases. Tables report 2022–2023 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by issuer and instrument, and secured funding issuance and maturities, including card securitizations, FHLB advances, First Republic’s Purchase Money Note, and other secured funding. Client-driven loan securitizations are excluded because they are not Firm funding.

nodes.title: Long-Term Funding and Issuance
nodes.summary: The Firm’s long-term funding plan supports stable funding and liquidity, guided by client activity, liquidity, regulatory requirements including TLAC, diversification, market access, and cost optimization across markets, tenors, and currencies. Most outstanding long-term debt is issued by the Parent Company, which advances substantially all net proceeds to the IHC; the IHC issues no external debt. Higher year-end 2023 structured notes reflected Markets client-driven net issuance and fair-value increases. Tables report 2023 and 2022 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by entity and debt type, including TLAC-eligible notes. The Firm also obtains secured long-term funding through credit-card securitizations and FHLB advances; related issuance and maturities, including First Republic FHLB advances and a Purchase Money Note, are summarized.

nodes.title: Long-term secured funding
nodes.summary: The table reports long-term secured funding by type—credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, the First Republic-related Purchase Money Note, and other secured funding, including secured structured notes—showing issuances and maturities/redemptions for 2022 and 2023 (in millions). Client-driven loan securitizations are excluded because they are not a Firm funding source; further details are in Notes 14 and 34.

The section describes the Firm’s funding strategy, capacity, and sources, including deposits, capital-market borrowing, and equity, and how bank and non-bank subsidiaries fund themselves. It reports deposit balances, trends, drivers, rates, uninsured deposits, maturities, and loan-to-deposit metrics. It also details non-deposit funding balances and composition, short-term secured and unsecured borrowing, and long-term funding plans, issuance, maturities, and redemptions by instrument and issuer, including structured notes, securitizations, FHLB advances, and First Republic-related funding.

nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.summary: Credit-rating downgrades may reduce liquidity and funding access, raise costs, trigger collateral or funding demands, deter lenders, and affect VIE and third-party commitments; the Firm says stress metrics account for these effects and liquidity is sufficient. The text lists 2023 ratings and outlook changes, notes unsecured debt has no rating-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits, or collateral clauses, and outlines factors agencies assess. It defines reputation risk, its potential causes and harms, describes independent risk-management governance and oversight, and assigns all business units and employees responsibility for considering reputational effects, including environmental and social concerns.

Covers liquidity-risk definitions, governance, oversight, centralized management and stress testing, and contingency funding strategies. Reports LCR and HQLA requirements, levels and trends, available securities, cash and borrowing capacity, and NSFR compliance. Describes funding strategy and sources, including deposits, market borrowing, equity, short- and long-term instruments, balances and trends. Also discusses credit-rating effects, ratings and agency factors, liquidity protections, and reputational-risk governance and responsibilities.

nodes.title: Reputation Risk Management
nodes.summary: Reputation risk arises when actions or inactions harm perceptions of the Firm’s integrity or competence among stakeholders. It can stem from employees, strategies, activities, or business relationships and may cause financial, legal, regulatory, or other harm. An independent risk function maintains firmwide governance policy and standards and oversees processes for identifying, escalating, and monitoring issues. The policy sets management principles; all business units, corporate functions, and employees must consider reputation when evaluating products, transactions, relationships, jurisdictions, processes, and other activities. Environmental and social concerns are increasingly important considerations.

Explains strategic risk from flawed plans or inadequate responses to change and its governance, identification, initiative assessment, and integration into planning and budgeting. Covers capital risk oversight, strategy, planning, stress testing, contingency actions, regulatory frameworks and requirements, capital measures and allocation, distributions, debt, and subsidiary needs, including Federal Reserve CCAR results. Describes liquidity governance, stress testing, funding plans and sources, regulatory ratios, available resources, and credit-rating effects. Outlines reputation-risk causes and impacts, firmwide policies and responsibilities for identifying, escalating, and monitoring issues, including environmental and social considerations.

nodes.title: Credit and Investment Risk Management
Credit Risk Management and Measurement
nodes.summary: The page describes credit and investment risks across consumer and wholesale lending, client activities, investment securities, and bank deposits. It outlines firmwide credit governance, including policies, exposure approvals, concentration limits, underwriting, delinquency management, loss estimates, and capital management. Credit risk is measured using default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default, with allowances covering loans, commitments, and securities; capital addresses unexpected losses. Stress testing applies economic and business scenarios to assess losses, credit migration, delinquency trends, industries, countries, and counterparties, informing risk appetite.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.summary: The text defines credit and investment risk, covering defaults or credit-profile changes and losses or reduced returns across consumer, wholesale, and investment exposures. It describes the Firm’s credit risk governance: policies, portfolio monitoring and approvals, concentration limits, underwriting, authority assignment, management of troubled exposures, loss estimates, and capital support. Risk measurement uses default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default to estimate allowances and capital needs. Stress testing evaluates macroeconomic and other scenarios, potential credit migration and losses, and informs risk appetite and counterparty decisions.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and management
nodes.summary: The Firm’s credit-risk framework safeguards independent, accurate approval and active monitoring at transaction and portfolio levels through approval authorities, concentration limits, risk-rating methods, reviews, distressed-exposure guidelines, and independent validation of certain models and assumptions. Consumer risk monitoring tracks delinquency, trends, and concentrations against expectations, economic forecasts, and industry benchmarks, informing underwriting and loss estimates. Wholesale risk is monitored across portfolios, industries, and counterparties, with periodically reviewed limits and stress-based loss constraints; exposures are managed through underwriting, syndications, sales, securitizations, derivatives, netting, collateral, and other mitigants. Independent Credit Review assesses wholesale risk grades and their timeliness, and evaluates credit processes, analyses, LGD rationales, monitoring, and policy compliance. Note 12 provides further loan details.

nodes.title: Risk reporting
nodes.summary: Credit risk is monitored through regular reporting to senior Credit Risk Management on aggregate exposures, credit quality forecasts, concentrations and risk profile changes. Detailed portfolio reports cover industries, clients, counterparties, customers, products and geographies. Senior management reviews the adequacy of credit loss allowances at least quarterly, while risk trends and limit exceptions are regularly reported to and discussed by risk committees, senior management and the Board.

nodes.title: Credit Portfolio
nodes.summary: Defines credit risk and the loans and exposures included or excluded from the credit-portfolio tables, with references to related notes and consumer, wholesale, securities, and financing disclosures. Explains the 2023 adoption of guidance replacing TDR disclosures with financial-difficulty modification disclosures. Reports 2023 and 2022 credit portfolio assets, commitments, exposure-management instruments, and nonperforming assets, with notes on margin receivables, First Republic exposure, and exclusions. Also gives nonaccrual loans and ratios, plus net charge-offs, average retained loans, and charge-off rates.

nodes.title: Consumer Credit Portfolio
Consumer Credit Portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: The Firm’s retained consumer portfolio primarily includes loans and lending commitments for residential real estate, credit cards, scored auto, and business banking, including First Republic exposures, mainly residential real estate. It also includes loans at fair value, predominantly residential real estate. The Firm focuses on prime consumers; originated mortgages are retained, securitized, or sold to U.S. government agencies or government-sponsored enterprises, while other consumer loans are generally retained. Notes 12 and 28 provide details on consumer loans and lending commitments. Tables present scored consumer credit portfolio information for CCB, AWM, CIB, and Corporate.

nodes.title: Consumer credit portfolio
nodes.summary: Presents the consumer credit portfolio at December 31, 2023 and 2022: credit exposure and nonaccrual loans for residential real estate, auto and other, consumer loans excluding credit cards, credit cards, commitments, total consumer exposure, and credit-related notes. Reports annual net charge-offs or recoveries, average retained loans, and charge-off rates. Footnotes define included products and commitments, excluded operating lease assets and certain loans, First Republic exposure, nonaccrual policy and exclusions, credit protection notes, and loans excluded from charge-off-rate calculations.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: The table presents December 31, 2023 consumer-loan maturities by scheduled repayment period, loan class, and fixed or variable interest-rate terms.
