Figures are in millions. Footnotes identify First Republic loans included in specified maturity periods, explain treatment of loans that reset from fixed to variable rates, and note that within-one-year amounts include held-for-sale and fair-value loans and that credit card amounts include overdrafts.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards grew in 2023, mainly from First Republic residential real estate loans and auto originations. The text describes residential portfolio composition and changes, including interest-only mortgages, HELOC balances and risk controls, government-guaranteed loan delinquency data, geographic concentration and improved LTVs, and modified loans. Auto and other loans increased overall, while auto charge-offs rose with used-car value declines. Tables report nonperforming assets and nonaccrual loan activity for 2023 and 2022, with exclusions and references to further credit-quality information in Note 12.

nodes.title: Credit Card
key_items: Geographic and FICO composition of credit card loans

Loans generally remain on accrual until charge-off, with the allowance covering estimated uncollectible accrued and billed interest and fees. Five states held 46% of the portfolio. Credit card FDMs were $648 million, with $27 million in trial modifications; prior-year TDRs were $418 million, and accounting changes ended TDR concession assessments. The wholesale portfolio’s exposures, active risk management, and First Republic integration are described. In 2023, retained loans and lending commitments rose, largely due to First Republic; nonperforming exposure increased, while wholesale charge-offs rose from restructuring and losses in real estate, consumer and retail. A table presents 2023 and 2022 wholesale credit assets, commitments, portfolio totals, credit-risk-management instruments, and footnotes on customer receivables, derivatives, and First Republic exposure.

Describes the Firm’s consumer portfolio—primarily prime residential real estate, credit cards, auto and business-banking loans and commitments, including First Republic exposures—and how loans are retained, securitized or sold. Tables report portfolio exposures, nonaccrual loans, commitments, charge-offs, recoveries, average loans, rates and maturities by loan type and interest terms, with definitions and exclusions. The section reviews consumer-loan growth, mortgage composition, HELOC controls, delinquencies, geography, LTVs, modifications and auto losses; credit-card growth, credit quality, charge-offs, FDMs and modifications; and wholesale exposures, risk management, First Republic integration, nonperforming assets, commitments, credit-risk instruments and losses.

nodes.title: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
Wholesale credit portfolio
nodes.summary: The discussion outlines wholesale credit-risk sources, portfolio retention and syndication, active reviews of borrower quality, collateral, and concentrations, and coverage across business segments; First Republic integration may alter classifications and ratings. In 2023, retained loans rose $68.8 billion and lending commitments $64.8 billion, mainly due to First Republic. Nonperforming exposure rose $476 million, while net charge-offs increased $698 million, driven by a loan restructuring and losses in Real Estate (especially Office) and Consumer & Retail. A table reports 2023 and 2022 portfolio assets, commitments, credit exposure, and nonperforming amounts, with notes defining customer receivables and credit-derivative measures and identifying $90.6 billion of First Republic exposure.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale credit portfolio maturity and internal ratings profiles at December 31, 2023 and 2022, including retained loans, derivatives net of collateral, lending commitments, loans held for sale or at fair value, customer receivables, total exposure, and credit-risk management derivatives and notes. Ratings classify BBB-/Baa3-equivalent or higher as investment grade, considering collateral and structural support. Footnotes explain loan composition, credit derivatives and ratings, purchased protection, and maturity methodology; investment-grade exposure shares are reported.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.summary: The Firm manages and diversifies industry exposures, focusing on sectors with actual or potential credit concerns. Criticized exposures follow U.S. banking regulators’ special mention, substandard, and doubtful categories. Excluding loans held-for-sale and at fair value, criticized exposure rose from $31.3 billion (2.7% of wholesale credit exposure) in 2022 to $41.4 billion (3.3%) in 2023; $38.3 billion was performing. The increase primarily reflected downgrades in Real Estate, Technology, Media & Telecommunications (mainly Technology), and Healthcare. An industry table presents exposures at both year-ends; risk-industry classification generally reflects clients’ or counterparties’ primary business activity. See Note 4 for concentration details.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industries (a)
nodes.summary: The text presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 and 2022 wholesale credit exposure by industry and credit-quality category, with selected metrics including investment- and noninvestment-grade, criticized and noncriticized exposures, delinquent loans, collateral, credit derivatives, and net charge-offs/recoveries. Notes explain rankings, category definitions, exclusions, state and municipal securities, First Republic exposure, and credit-risk mitigation. It then details Real Estate exposure by property type for both years, including lending commitments, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade and drawn percentages, changes in criticized exposure, and related geographic, collateral, and First Republic disclosures.

nodes.title: Real Estate
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 and 2022 credit exposures for Real Estate, Consumer & Retail, and Oil & Gas, including loans and lending commitments, derivative receivables, total credit exposure, investment-grade shares, and drawn ratios. It notes changes in criticized exposure and their drivers, plus industry-specific collateral, portfolio composition, and geographic or borrower details: Real Estate’s multifamily concentration in California and First Republic exposure; Consumer & Retail category definitions and Leisure collateralization; and Oil & Gas subsectors, secured lending, and investment-grade unsecured exposure.

nodes.title: Consumer & Retail
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2023, Consumer & Retail credit exposure was $127.1 billion, up from $120.6 billion a year earlier; criticized exposure rose $409 million to $8.3 billion, as client-specific downgrades were mostly offset by upgrades and portfolio activity. The text details 2023 and 2022 exposure by five subsectors, loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade shares, and drawn ratios, plus security and portfolio-composition notes. Oil & Gas exposure was $34.5 billion, including $123 million criticized, down from $38.7 billion in 2022. Comparable metrics are given for E&P and oil field services, other Oil & Gas, and totals; notes describe subsector definitions, secured and unsecured shares, reserve-based lending, and drawn ratios.

nodes.title: Oil & Gas
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 and 2022 Consumer & Retail and Oil & Gas credit exposure by subsector, including loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, total exposure, investment-grade shares, and drawn percentages. It notes criticized-exposure trends, collateralization and unsecured-credit quality, and defines the subsectors. It also describes wholesale loans and refers readers to loan-credit-quality disclosures, then presents 2023–2022 nonaccrual loan activity and net charge-offs/recoveries and rates, explains drivers of nonaccrual growth, and reports modified wholesale FDM and prior-period TDR balances and the effect of changed modification rules.

nodes.title: Wholesale Loans and Credit Loss Activity
nodes.summary: The page describes wholesale lending to corporate, institutional, and high-net-worth clients and refers readers to Note 12 for credit quality details. It reports nonaccrual loan activity for 2023 and 2022: balances rose $319 million in 2023, mainly from Real Estate, Healthcare, and Individuals, partly offset by an upgrade. It also presents average retained loans, gross charge-offs and recoveries, net charge-offs or recoveries, and related rates, excluding nonaccrual-loan sale gains or losses.

nodes.title: Modified wholesale loans
nodes.summary: Wholesale modified loans (FDMs) had an amortized cost of $2.1 billion in 2023; wholesale TDRs totaled $801 million in 2022. Because the requirement to assess whether modifications were reasonably expected or involved a concession was eliminated, the FDM population is larger than the population previously classified as TDRs. Notes 1 and 12 provide further information, including on prior-period TDRs.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 wholesale loan maturities by class and fixed or variable rate, including First Republic amounts and notes on rate resets and included loan types. It gives 2022–2023 net charge-offs or recoveries, average retained loans, and rates by loan class. It explains that contractual wholesale lending commitments may overstate expected exposure because they are often unused or expire, and describes collateral, monitoring, and loss allowances for customer margin receivables. It also covers derivatives’ risk-management uses, counterparty exposures, netting and collateral protections, 87% OTC collateral-agreement coverage, derivative receivables falling from $70.9 billion in 2022 to $54.9 billion in 2023 mainly due to market movements, and additional collateral held against potential exposure.

nodes.title: Lending Commitments and Customer Receivables
nodes.summary: The Firm’s lending commitments and guarantees support client financing; their contractual amounts are maximum potential credit exposure but generally do not reflect expected exposure or funding needs because they are often unused, refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expired. Customer receivables are collateralized brokerage margin loans, managed through margin requirements and monitoring. Short-term loans, collateral value, and margin calls generally mitigate risk, so allowances are typically unnecessary; when needed, expected losses reflect collateral value and default probability. Receivables appear in accrued interest and accounts receivable. Notes 28 and 13 provide further information on commitments and credit-loss allowance policies, respectively.

nodes.title: Derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The Firm uses derivatives for client risk management, market-making and its own risk control, with counterparty or CCP credit risk depending on settlement type. It mitigates exposure through netting and collateral; about 87% of eligible OTC trades were collateralized in 2023 and 2022. Net derivative receivables fell from $70.9 billion in 2022 to $54.9 billion in 2023, primarily due to market movements; tables detail collateral offsets and ratings profiles. Additional collateral may secure potential exposure. The Firm measures future credit risk using Peak, DRE and AVG, which support limits, aggregation, pricing, capital and CVA. Risk management addresses wrong-way risk and hedges CVA. Exposure projections generally decline after year one absent new trades.

nodes.title: Derivative Receivables and Credit Risk
nodes.summary: Tables present 2023 and 2022 net derivative receivables after cash and other collateral, and investment-grade versus noninvestment-grade exposure shares. The text explains Peak, DRE, and AVG measures of potential credit loss and their uses in limits, risk aggregation, pricing, capital, and CVA. It describes CVA, active risk management and wrong-way risk adjustments, hedging CVA changes with derivatives, and projected exposure profiles, which generally decline after year one absent new trades.

nodes.title: Exposure profile of derivatives measures
nodes.summary: The text presents a 2023 derivatives exposure profile by maturity (1, 2, 5, and 10 years, plus average and peak). It explains that JPMorgan uses credit derivatives as a market-maker and to manage its own credit risk. Credit portfolio management derivatives mitigate risks from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale derivative counterparty exposures; other end-user derivatives manage risks such as certain market-making securities and are excluded from this category. Net protection purchased or sold for portfolio management totaled $37.0 billion in 2023, versus $18.1 billion in 2022, including loan-related protection of $24.2 billion ($6.4 billion in 2022) and derivative-receivable protection of $12.8 billion ($11.7 billion). These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are fair-valued through principal transactions revenue, while the managed loans and commitments use accrual accounting, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall exposure changes. CDS hedging effectiveness can differ because of reference entities, contractual credit-event terms, and maturity mismatches; the Firm generally aligns protection maturity with exposure and actively monitors remaining differences.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.summary:
Management’s discussion and analysis
Credit derivatives
The Firm uses credit derivatives for two primary purposes: first, in its capacity as a market-maker, and second, as an end-user to manage the Firm’s own credit risk associated with various exposures.

nodes.title: Credit portfolio management activities
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives to mitigate risks from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale derivatives counterparty exposure; other credit derivatives hedge certain market-making securities but are excluded from this category. Net protection purchased or sold was $36.989 billion in 2023 versus $18.143 billion in 2022, covering loans and commitments ($24.157 billion; $6.422 billion) and derivative receivables ($12.832 billion; $11.721 billion). These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are fair-valued through principal transactions revenue, while managed loans and commitments use accrual accounting, creating earnings volatility. CDS hedging effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, contract terms, or maturity mismatches; the Firm generally aligns maturities and monitors and manages remaining differences.

Describes wholesale credit-risk management, portfolio composition and growth, First Republic integration, exposure by maturity, rating, industry and key sectors, and changes in criticized and nonperforming exposures, charge-offs, and recoveries. Covers wholesale loan maturities, nonaccrual and modified loans, commitments, guarantees, and collateralized customer receivables. Explains derivative counterparty exposure, collateral and netting, ratings and potential-exposure measures, wrong-way risk and CVA hedging, plus credit-derivative protection activity, accounting treatment, and hedging limitations.

nodes.title: Allowance for Credit Losses
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
Allocation of allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses, its components and estimation using five weighted macroeconomic scenarios. It describes the 2023 $3.1 billion net increase to $24.8 billion, driven by consumer and wholesale portfolio changes and First Republic, plus a $587 million reduction from updated TDR accounting. It provides central and adverse economic forecasts, notes future estimate updates, and presents 2022–2023 tables detailing allowance balances, provisions, charge-offs, recoveries, impairment methods, retained loans, credit ratios, and loan-class allocations, with related footnotes and references.

nodes.title: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text outlines investment portfolio risks, distinguishing high-quality Treasury/CIO securities from long-term principal investments. It reports the securities portfolio’s $569.2 billion carrying value and AA+ average rating at year-end 2023, and principal investment values of $39.3 billion in 2023 versus $37.0 billion in 2022, including tax-oriented and private equity/debt/real-asset holdings. It describes governance, independent valuation reviews, risk limits, and stress testing. Market risk management covers its responsibilities, measurement tools (including VaR, stress tests, drawdowns, and sensitivity measures), limit-setting and breach escalation, and model uncertainty and ongoing metric reviews.

Covers credit and investment risk definitions, governance, measurement, stress testing, monitoring, reporting, and risk controls. Details consumer and wholesale portfolios, including exposures, commitments, credit quality, delinquencies, nonperforming assets, charge-offs, modifications, collateral, derivatives, and risk mitigants, with portfolio tables and accounting disclosures. Explains credit-loss allowance estimation, economic scenarios, balances, and changes. Describes investment holdings, valuation oversight, risk limits, and market-risk tools such as VaR, stress tests, drawdowns, and sensitivity measures.

nodes.title: Market Risk Management
Market Risk Management and Measurement
key_items: Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.summary: Market risk arises when market factors—including interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities—change the value of assets and liabilities. Market Risk Management establishes policies, independently measures, monitors and controls risk across business lines and the Firm, sets and oversees limits, conducts stress tests and qualitative assessments, and supports efficient risk-return decisions, lower performance volatility, and transparency for senior leaders, the Board, and regulators. Because no single metric captures market risk, it uses statistical and nonstatistical measures, including value-at-risk, stress testing, profit-and-loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, economic value sensitivity, and other sensitivity measures.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and control
nodes.summary: Market risk is controlled through firm-, business-line, corporate- and entity-level limits, including VaR, stress and other measures. Limits are reviewed, approved, monitored and escalated; breaches prompt corrective action or temporary increases, while model uncertainty and periodic measure enhancements are recognized. The text maps each business’s activities, market risks, positions captured by VaR, earnings-at-risk and sensitivity measures, including principal investments. It explains Risk Management VaR’s historical-simulation framework, uses, limitations, proxies, data differences and periodic updates, and distinguishes Regulatory VaR’s Basel III scope, assumptions and capital role.

nodes.title: VaR
Value-at-risk
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its historical-simulation VaR framework, used across the Firm to measure and aggregate market risk, monitor limits, and report results. Risk Management VaR uses a one-day holding period and approximately 95% expected-tail-loss confidence level; Regulatory VaR, for Basel III capital on covered positions, uses ten business days and approximately 99%, with different position coverage and diversification treatment. VaR’s historical-data, liquidity, proxy, and horizon limitations are addressed with stress testing and other measures; data sources may differ from valuation testing, and models are periodically reviewed and updated. Tables and a graph present 2023 and 2022 VaR by risk type and business, including diversification and explanatory notes. Average total VaR fell $15 million in 2023, mainly due to lower volatility and reduced fixed-income, commodities, and equities risk; 2022 nickel-market volatility drove unusually high maxima.

nodes.title: Total VaR
nodes.summary: The text presents the Firm’s 95%-confidence Risk Management VaR results for 2023 and 2022, including average, minimum and maximum VaR by CIB trading risk type, Credit Portfolio, CIB, CCB, Corporate and other, and total VaR. It notes that VaR changes with positions, volatility and diversification. Footnotes explain diversification calculations and limits, Credit Portfolio VaR scope and the removal of certain CVA exposures and related hedges, a legacy publicly traded private-equity position, and elevated March 2022 maxima caused by nickel-market volatility. Average Total VaR fell $15 million in 2023, mainly due to lower volatility and risk reductions in fixed income, commodities and equities; a graph of daily VaR over the four trailing quarters is referenced.

nodes.title: Daily Risk Management VaR
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s daily Risk Management VaR backtesting and the chart of quarterly VaR levels. Backtesting compares daily VaR with gains and losses defined consistently with Basel III, excluding several revenue components, so results may differ from reported revenue and CIB Markets loss days. An exception is a loss exceeding the prior day’s VaR; five per 100 trading days are statistically expected, though volatility changes can affect the count. In 2023, the Firm had gains on 139 of 258 days and 13 exceptions, eight in the fourth quarter. A chart shows trailing-year and three-month loss distributions as percentages of VaR, grouped in 50-point intervals, with exceptions above 100%; results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory VaR backtesting.

nodes.title: Distribution of Daily Backtesting Gains and Losses
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan’s risk measures: stress testing complements VaR by assessing hypothetical simultaneous market shocks, including rallies, sell-offs, tail events, geographic and asset-class risks, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risk. Results inform exposure analysis, limits, CCAR, risk appetite, and reporting to senior management and board committees; Market Risk Management oversees the framework, models, and methodology changes. Profit-and-loss drawdowns flag revenue declines from year-to-date peaks beyond tolerance levels. Structural interest rate risk arises from trading and banking activities. Governance, limits, oversight, and management responsibilities are described, along with key drivers such as repricing and maturity mismatches, yield-curve changes, and rate-driven changes in maturities. The Firm manages exposure centrally, transferring business-unit risk to Treasury and CIO via funds transfer pricing that accounts for balances, rates, payment schedules, prepayments, repricing terms, indices, and rate caps or floors.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s historical-simulation VaR framework, its Risk Management and Basel III Regulatory measures, coverage and limitations, model governance, and 2023–2022 results by risk type and business. Results explain diversification, key footnotes, the decline in average total VaR, and elevated 2022 maxima from nickel volatility. Covers daily VaR backtesting methods, exceptions and loss distributions, plus complementary stress testing, drawdown monitoring, and structural interest-rate risk drivers, governance, and centralized transfer of exposure to Treasury and CIO.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
key_items: Other risk measures Stress testing; Profit and loss drawdowns; Structural interest rate risk management
Key Risk Drivers and Risk Management Process
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s earnings-at-risk method for assessing structural interest-rate exposure, including modeled assets, liabilities, exclusions, 12-month baseline sensitivities, parallel and yield-curve scenarios, and assumptions about balance sheets, prepayments, reinvestment, deposits, and deposit betas. It describes a 2023 model update for deposit repricing lags, sensitivity testing and governance, reported U.S.- and non-U.S.-dollar scenario results, and drivers of year-over-year changes, including the First Republic acquisition. It notes earnings-at-risk is not an income forecast and introduces Economic Value Sensitivity (EVS), its balance-sheet scope, stress testing, and limits relative to tangible common equity.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. Dollar FX Risk
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk arises when exchange-rate changes affect the Firm’s assets, liabilities, or future results. Structural exposures come from capital investments, forecast expenses and revenues, investment securities, and foreign-currency debt. Treasury and CIO, partnering with the LOBs, primarily manage these risks and may hedge some with derivatives. Further information is referenced in Business Segment Results on page 66.

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.summary: The text reports sensitivities for market-risk exposures excluded from VaR and earnings-at-risk, describing affected activities, measures, 2023/2022 impacts, hedge netting, limitations, and accounting destinations (net revenue, OCI, or noninterest expense), with notes on excluded securities and CVA governance. It then explains country risk management: its purpose, independent governance and responsibilities; sources of exposure and country-attribution rules; exposure scope, exclusions, assumptions, and measurement methods for deposits, lending, securities financing, securities, derivatives, and credit derivatives; and differences from FFIEC reporting.

Explains how market risk arises and how the Firm governs, measures, monitors and controls it through limits, escalation, stress tests and multiple statistical and sensitivity measures. Covers Risk Management and Regulatory VaR frameworks, results, diversification, backtesting, limitations and model governance; structural interest-rate risk, earnings-at-risk assumptions and results, and economic value sensitivity; non-U.S.-dollar FX exposures and hedging; other sensitivity-based exposures, impacts and accounting treatment; and country-risk governance, attribution, exposure measurement, exclusions and differences from FFIEC reporting.

nodes.title: Country Risk Management
nodes.summary: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s country-risk framework: independent oversight, policies, sovereign ratings, limits, surveillance, exposure monitoring, and scenario analysis. Explains country attribution and measurement across deposits, lending, securities financing, securities, derivatives, and credit derivatives, noting exclusions, assumptions, and differences from FFIEC reporting. Covers tailored stress testing and regular reporting, including separate reporting for certain territories. Presents 2023 and comparative 2022 top-20 non-U.S. country exposures by category, explains changes in Japan and Australia, reports approximately $350 million exposure to Russia with a specified deposit exclusion, and provides table scope and category/ranking footnotes.

nodes.title: Climate Risk Management
nodes.summary: Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the Firm, distinguishing acute and chronic physical risks from transition risks driven by policy, technology, consumer shifts, and physical change. Describes Climate Risk Management’s firmwide framework, policies, metrics, scenarios, data and technology strategy, while businesses identify and manage risks and report significant matters to the Board Risk Committee. Defines operational risk and outlines the CCOR framework, governance and responsibilities, self-assessments and independent oversight, qualitative and quantitative measurement using LDA and AMA capital methods, stress testing, and ongoing monitoring and control testing.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Management
Operational Risk Management Framework
key_items: Operational Risk Governance; Operational Risk Identification; Operational Risk Measurement
Management of Operational Risk; Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.summary: The text defines operational risk, its sources and manifestations, and the aim of managing it in line with the Firm’s circumstances. It describes the CCOR framework and governance responsibilities, including Board oversight and independent CCOR leadership; risk identification through self-assessments and independent challenge; measurement through control reviews, loss estimates, the LDA model, AMA capital methodology, and stress testing; monitoring and testing of compliance and controls; remediation through action plans; and firmwide reporting, risk indicators, appetite assessments, and escalation to committees, senior management, and the Board.

nodes.title: Insurance
nodes.summary:
Insurance
One of the ways in which operational risk may be mitigated is through insurance maintained by the Firm. The Firm purchases insurance from commercial insurers and maintains a wholly-owned captive insurer, Park Assurance Company. Insurance may also be required by third parties with whom the Firm does business.

nodes.title: Subcategories and examples of operational risks
key_items: War in Ukraine and Sanctions; Business and technology resiliency risk; Payment fraud risk
nodes.summary: The text outlines operational-risk categories and examples: evolving Ukraine-related sanctions and compliance controls; business and technology resiliency planning for disruptions; payment-fraud controls and education; and third-party oversight to manage performance, data-loss and continuity risks. It defines cybersecurity risk, describes threats from geopolitical attacks, suppliers and clients, security measures and potential impacts. It also details the CISO-led Information Security Program and its operations, governance, risk-control, awareness and technology-resiliency functions; incident response and external collaboration; independent assessment; management committees and escalation; and periodic Board, Audit Committee and Risk Committee oversight.

nodes.title: Compliance Risk Management
nodes.summary: Compliance risk is the risk of failing to meet applicable laws, regulations, codes, or standards. Business lines and Corporate own and manage this risk, while the independent Operational Risk and Compliance organization oversees, monitors, tests, and reports on it through policies and standards. Risks span products, customer relationships, employee activities, AML, trading, market conduct, cross-border services, and fiduciary duties; other functions oversee obligations in their areas. Governance is coordinated through the CCOR Management Framework, led by the Global CCO and relevant risk executive, with significant issues reported to Board Risk and Audit Committees. The Code of Conduct requires integrity, prompt reporting of violations or unethical conduct, onboarding and periodic training, and annual employee affirmation. Reports can be made globally through an externally administered, anonymous where legally permitted hotline; retaliation for good-faith reporting or assistance is prohibited, and the Audit Committee periodically receives program reports.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk Management
nodes.summary: Conduct risk is operational risk arising from employee actions or misconduct that may cause unfair customer outcomes, undermine market integrity, harm employees or the Firm, or damage its reputation. Each line of business and Corporate is responsible for managing this risk and fostering a culture aligned with the Firm’s Business Principles and Code, which guide ethical, legally compliant conduct. The CCOR Management Framework coordinates oversight; a senior forum connects initiatives, identifies emerging risks, sets strategic direction, and reviews the Firmwide Conduct Risk Appetite Assessment. Management spans the employee life cycle, and business units and designated functions periodically assess risk, review metrics and issues, and provide education.

nodes.title: Legal Risk Management
nodes.summary: Legal risk is operational risk arising from actual or alleged failure to meet legal obligations under applicable law, agreements, or the Firm’s products and services. The global Legal function manages litigation, enforcement, investigations, disputes, contracts, product and business advice, legal interpretation and advocacy, and advice to business units, Corporate, and the Board; it also selects and manages outside counsel and advises the Conflicts Office on potentially conflicting wholesale transactions. The General Counsel reports to the CEO, serves on key firmwide committees, and, with Legal colleagues, reports significant matters to the Board and Audit Committee. Legal also advises committees and business units on potential reputational risks.

nodes.title: Estimations and Model Risk Management
nodes.summary: Estimation and model risk is operational risk arising when decisions rely on incorrect or misused outputs. The Firm uses estimates and models for valuation, risk, capital, stress testing, credit-loss allowances and business decisions; independent MRGR governs related policies and review. Business users and developers own model risk, develop, test, submit models for approval, maintain and monitor them, and may enhance them. MRGR-approved tiers reflect complexity, exposure and reliance; reviews assess suitability, methods and assumptions and may require testing or back-testing. New and materially changed models generally require prior approval, though exceptions may involve interim risk controls. Uncertainty can rise when market conditions differ from historical data or acquired assets differ from model-development inputs, requiring more judgment in adjusting outputs. The text refers readers to critical accounting estimates and Note 2 for valuation methods.

Explains the Firm’s operational risk framework, governance, identification, measurement, monitoring, remediation, reporting and escalation, and mitigation through commercial insurance and a captive insurer. Covers key operational risks including sanctions, resilience, payment fraud, third parties and cybersecurity, alongside information-security controls and oversight. Describes compliance, conduct and legal risk responsibilities, governance, employee standards and reporting. Also addresses estimation and model risk, including ownership, independent review and approval, uncertainty, and accounting-estimate references.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide risk framework, shared accountability, risk appetite, three lines of defense, and Board and management governance, committees, escalation, and oversight. Covers strategic, capital, liquidity, and reputation risks; credit and investment exposures, controls, loss allowances, and valuation; market risk measurement, interest rates, foreign exchange, and country exposures; climate risks; and operational, compliance, conduct, legal, cybersecurity, resilience, third-party, and model-estimation risks, including their governance, measurement, stress testing, monitoring, reporting, and mitigation.

nodes.title: Critical Accounting Estimates Used by the Firm
Allowance for credit losses
key_items: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase explains that critical accounting estimates rely on controlled, independently reviewed, consistent methods and management judgment. Its allowance for credit losses covers amortized-cost financial assets and certain lending commitments, comprising loan, commitment, and investment-securities allowances. Estimates depend on forecasts, loss history, risk and collateral assessments, and expected lives. The eight-quarter forecast uses hundreds of macroeconomic variables; key consumer and wholesale drivers are identified. First Republic acquired wholesale exposures were assessed using comparable facilities rather than modeled estimates, while most consumer exposures were modeled. A comparison of central and adverse scenarios illustrates sensitivity: adverse assumptions raise modeled losses by about $850 million for residential real estate, $3.1 billion for credit cards, and $3.9 billion for wholesale exposures. These figures are not forecasts or estimates of total allowance changes, given scenario weighting, interacting nonlinear variables, portfolio and borrower changes, and qualitative adjustments. The Firm considers its governance and 2023 estimates reasonable.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase measures most fair-value assets and liabilities recurringly, including derivatives, structured notes and securities financing agreements; some collateral-based loans are measured nonrecurringly. The 2023 table reports fair-value assets by category and hierarchy level, totaling $1.134 trillion, including $26.1 billion in Level 3; Level 3 equals 1% of total Firm assets and 2% of fair-value assets. A footnote explains derivative netting treatment. Valuation requires judgment based on market observability, model choice, empirical inputs and adjustments for credit, funding, liquidity and risk. Uncertainty, illiquidity and differing methods or assumptions can affect estimates and recorded gains or losses; Note 2 provides further details.

nodes.title: Goodwill impairment
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP requires goodwill to be allocated to reporting units and tested for impairment at least annually; the Firm’s methodology is described in Note 15. Management uses significant judgment, reviewing economic conditions, estimated cost of equity, actual results, and performance projections. In 2023, it concluded goodwill was not impaired: each reporting unit’s fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 9%, with no significant risk indicated by current projections and valuations. Projections reflect management’s short-term outlook and long-term growth and return-on-equity estimates, benchmarked against third-party and peer data where possible. Note 15 provides further details.

nodes.title: Credit card rewards liability
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase cardholders earn generally unlimited, non-expiring rewards points redeemable for cash or account credits, gift cards, and travel. The Firm accrues an estimated liability as points are earned and reduces it upon redemption; recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities, it was $13.2 billion at year-end 2023, up from $11.3 billion in 2022, mainly due to points earned on higher spending and promotions exceeding redemptions, and partly to program-term changes. The estimate depends on redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions, periodically reviewed using historical results, customer behavior, and management judgment. A 25-basis-point rise in redemption rate plus a 1-basis-point rise in cost per point would increase the 2023 liability by about $376 million.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s income tax accounting involves interpreting complex U.S. and foreign tax laws, estimating tax provisions and uncertain positions, and addressing disputes through audits, appeals, or courts; revised estimates may materially affect results. Deferred taxes reflect book–tax differences and enacted rates, with assets recognized when realization is more likely than not. The Firm reviews NOL and foreign tax credit carryforwards, future taxable income, and tax strategies, recording or reversing valuation allowances as warranted; at year-end 2023, deferred tax assets were expected to be realized, net of allowance. Unrecognized tax benefits are reassessed as information changes, and final tax outcomes or return-based adjustments can affect the provision and effective tax rate. Further details are in Note 25.

Litigation reserves

Management describes the purpose and limits of internal controls over financial reporting, reports an assessment under the COSO 2013 framework finding controls effective and no material weaknesses as of December 31, 2023, and notes PwC’s audit. The report is signed by CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum on February 16, 2024.

nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase management describes its responsibility for internal control over financial reporting, its purpose and key policies for accurate records, GAAP-compliant reporting, authorized transactions, and protecting assets. It notes inherent limitations and risks to future effectiveness. Using the COSO 2013 framework, management assessed controls as effective at December 31, 2023, with no material weaknesses. PwC audited their effectiveness. The report is signed by CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum and dated February 16, 2024.

key_items: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Fair Value of Certain Level 3 Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: PwC opines that JPMorgan Chase’s 2022–2023 balance sheets and 2021–2023 consolidated financial statements fairly present its results under U.S. GAAP, and that internal control over financial reporting was effective at year-end 2023. The report explains management and auditor responsibilities, PCAOB audit standards and procedures, and internal-control scope and limitations. It identifies two critical audit matters: estimating wholesale and credit-card loan-loss allowances, including economic forecasts and model adjustments, and valuing certain Level 3 instruments using significant unobservable inputs; it describes related control testing and audit procedures. PwC signed the report February 16, 2024, and notes it has served as auditor since 1965.

The auditor’s report is dated February 16, 2024, and states the firm has served since 1965. The text then presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 consolidated income statements, covering revenues, interest income and expense, credit-loss provisions, noninterest expenses, pretax income, taxes, net income, common-stockholder income, earnings per share, and weighted-average shares.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of income

The income statement covers revenue by source, net interest income, total revenue, credit-loss provisions, expense categories, pretax income, taxes, net income and common earnings, basic and diluted earnings per share, and weighted-average shares. The comprehensive income statement reports net income, after-tax other comprehensive gains or losses by category, and comprehensive income. Both statements note that the accompanying financial-statement notes are integral.

The balance sheets list assets, liabilities, commitments and contingencies, stockholders’ equity, and totals, with selected fair-value and pledged-asset details. nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets

Also reports assets and liabilities of consolidated variable interest entities (VIEs), explaining their settlement and limited-recourse characteristics. Shows 2021–2023 changes in stockholders’ equity, including share issuances, earnings, dividends, other comprehensive income, and treasury-stock activity, and notes accounting guidance adopted in 2023.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 consolidated statements of changes in stockholders’ equity, including preferred and common stock, paid-in capital, retained earnings, dividends, comprehensive income or loss, treasury stock, and total equity. It notes accounting guidance adopted in 2023 and refers readers to Note 1. It also provides 2021–2023 consolidated cash flows, detailing operating, investing, and financing activities, changes in cash, ending cash balances, and cash interest and income taxes paid.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of cash flows
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated cash flow statements present 2023, 2022 and 2021 figures (in millions) for operating activities, including net income and adjustments; investing activities, including securities, loans, the First Republic acquisition and other investments; and financing activities, including deposits, borrowings, stock transactions and dividends. They also report exchange-rate effects, changes in cash and bank deposits, beginning and ending balances, and cash interest and net income taxes paid. The accompanying notes are integral to the statements.

Reports the auditor’s fair-value audit procedures, report date, and tenure, followed by JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 consolidated income, comprehensive income, changes in stockholders’ equity, and cash flows, plus 2022–2023 balance sheets. Statements cover revenues, expenses, earnings per share, other comprehensive income, assets, liabilities, equity, financing and investing activities, and cash balances. Also includes consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and their limited-recourse characteristics, selected fair-value and pledged-asset details, accounting guidance adopted in 2023, and references to integral notes.

nodes.title: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
Note 1 - Basis of presentation
Consolidation
nodes.summary: Note 1 describes JPMorgan Chase’s business, the 2023 First Republic acquisition and ongoing integration, and its use of U.S. GAAP and applicable regulatory guidance. It explains consolidation policies for controlled entities, voting-interest entities, investment funds and variable-interest entities, including SPEs, primary-beneficiary tests and reassessments. It also covers interest and customer-contract revenue recognition, fair-value changes in principal transactions revenue, management estimates, foreign-currency translation and transaction accounting, and permitted balance-sheet offsetting under enforceable master netting agreements, which the Firm elects when conditions are met.
