It describes recognition of interest income and customer-contract and principal-transactions revenue, including related note references. It also covers estimates and assumptions in preparing consolidated statements and the translation of foreign-currency balances and transactions, including where resulting gains and losses are reported.

nodes.title: Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP allows qualifying derivatives, related cash collateral, and certain securities financing balances with the same counterparty to be presented net when specified conditions, including an enforceable master netting agreement, are met; the Firm elects net presentation where eligible. These agreements reduce counterparty credit risk by allowing transactions to be terminated, valued, and netted into one payment upon default. Associated collateral or margin agreements require net-deficit transfers, subject to thresholds, and allow the demanding party to set off amounts owed, liquidate collateral, and apply proceeds after default. See Notes 5 and 11 for details on derivatives and securities financing agreements.

nodes.title: Statements of cash flows
nodes.summary:
Statements of cash flows
For JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated statements of cash flows, cash is defined as those amounts included in cash and due from banks and deposits with banks on the Consolidated balance sheets.

nodes.title: Accounting standards adopted January 1, 2023
key_items: Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method
Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings (“TDRs”)
nodes.summary: Effective January 1, 2023, fair value hedging portfolio-layer guidance broadened eligible assets and hedges and clarified accounting presentation and disclosures. JPMorgan transferred HTM securities to AFS and designated them in portfolio-layer hedges; the retained-earnings impact was immaterial. TDR guidance eliminated TDR accounting and disclosures, permitted portfolio-based allowances, and changed DCF discount rates. The Firm adopted a non-DCF approach for most modified troubled loans, retaining DCF for collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans. Modified-retrospective adoption reduced credit-loss allowances by $587 million and increased after-tax retained earnings by $446 million. New disclosures cover specified modifications to financially distressed borrowers and gross charge-offs by origination vintage.

nodes.title: Significant accounting policies
nodes.summary: The section indexes JPMorgan Chase’s significant accounting policies and directs readers to detailed descriptions by note and page. Topics include fair value and its option, derivatives, revenue and expenses, interest, employee benefits and share-based incentives, investments, financing activities, loans and credit losses, variable interest entities, goodwill and other assets, property and leases, liabilities and debt, earnings per share, taxes, off-balance-sheet commitments, and litigation (Notes 2–30, pages 175–298).

Note 1 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s business, the First Republic acquisition and integration, U.S. GAAP basis, and consolidation policies for controlled entities, funds, SPEs, and VIEs, including primary-beneficiary assessments. It describes revenue recognition, fair-value changes, estimates, foreign-currency accounting, balance-sheet offsetting under enforceable netting agreements, and the definition of cash in cash-flow statements. It summarizes 2023 adoption of hedge and troubled-debt-modification standards and their effects and disclosures, and indexes significant accounting policies detailed in Notes 2–30.

nodes.title: Note 2 - Fair value measurement
Valuation process
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase measures some assets, liabilities and lending commitments at fair value, either recurrently or in specified circumstances. Fair value reflects an orderly market-participant transaction and uses quoted prices or valuation models with observable and unobservable inputs; estimates, judgments and methods can affect reported gains or losses. Risk-taking functions estimate values, while the independent Valuation Control Group verifies them, sets adjustments and conducts price verification; senior finance and risk executives oversee valuation through governance forums. Reviews use market data and, when unavailable, additional analyses and management review. Adjustments may address liquidity, large net open risk positions, uncertainty in unobservable inputs, counterparty and own credit risk (CVA/DVA), and funding (FVA); Level 1 quoted prices are not adjusted.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.summary: When market prices or comparable quotes are unavailable, fair value is generally estimated using valuation models based on transaction terms and market-based or independently sourced inputs, which undergo price verification. Under Firm policy, MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before implementation. Exceptions may permit interim use before approval, potentially subject to MRGR-required risk mitigations, such as restricting trading.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: Explains the U.S. GAAP three-level fair value hierarchy, defined by input observability, and classification by the lowest significant input level. It summarizes valuation methods and hierarchy classifications for securities financing, wholesale and consumer loans, securities, commodities, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, private equity and fund investments, VIE interests, and structured notes. Methods include quoted or comparable prices, broker quotes, discounted cash flows, models, NAV, and underlying-asset values; inputs and adjustments include credit, collateral, market, liquidity, prepayment, default, correlation, counterparty/funding, and own-credit factors. It also introduces fair-value asset and liability tables for 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s recurring fair-value assets and liabilities at December 31, 2023 and 2022, broken down by instrument and fair-value hierarchy levels 1–3, derivative netting adjustments, and total values. Notes explain mortgage-related GSE obligations, physical-commodity valuation, long/short securities presentation, investments using the NAV practical expedient, fair-valued mortgage loans, and derivative/collateral netting. The Level 3 discussion describes valuation governance, judgment and inputs, techniques and disclosures, and clarifies that input ranges and averages reflect instrument characteristics, not uncertainty or estimate reasonableness.

nodes.title: Fair value measurements using significant unobservable inputs
Level 3 valuations
nodes.summary: The text explains the Firm’s processes and judgment for valuing Level 3 instruments, including choosing valuation techniques and deriving significant unobservable inputs from empirical data. It describes how the disclosed input ranges and averages are calculated and cautions that they reflect instrument characteristics, not uncertainty or estimate reasonableness; Level 3 instruments may also contain observable components whose risks are managed with Level 1 and 2 positions. A 2023 table lists major Level 3 products, fair values, techniques, and unobservable inputs and ranges/averages. Footnotes explain aggregation, product composition, structured-note valuation, equity valuation methods, price conventions, and averaging methods.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.summary: Explains how changes in unobservable valuation inputs affect fair value, noting input interdependencies, generally applicable inverse relationships, and that observable–unobservable relationships are excluded. Defines yield and credit spreads and the instrument, collateral, borrower, and obligor factors shaping their ranges; prepayment speeds and their effects by premium/discount status; default rates and their links to collateral quality, prepayments, loss severity, and spreads; and loss severity and relevant mortgage factors. It also describes correlation and volatility inputs and their valuation effects and drivers, Bermudan swaption switch value, interest-rate curves, and forward prices and their determinants and potentially positive or negative fair-value effects.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.summary: Presents 2021–2023 rollforwards of Level 3 recurring fair-value assets and liabilities, including gains and losses, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and transfers, across trading securities, derivatives, AFS securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights, deposits, borrowings, trading liabilities, and other liabilities. Explains Level 3 classification, observable inputs and related hedging exclusions. Notes Level 3 shares of total fair-value assets and liabilities and clarifies net derivative presentation, income-statement/OCI reporting, immaterial AFS and DVA amounts, inclusion of loan originations in purchases, and items included in settlements.

nodes.title: Level 3 analysis
key_items: Consolidated balance sheets changes; For the year ended December 31, 2023
nodes.summary: The text reviews changes in recurring fair-value Level 3 assets since December 31, 2022, directing readers to separate disclosures for nonrecurring measurements and further details on MSRs. Level 3 assets ended 2023 at $23.7 billion, up $30 million: increases included non-trading loans, MSRs, and transfers from Level 2 as observability improved; these were largely offset by lower gross derivative receivables. It also lists significant 2022 transfers from Level 2 to Level 3 across debt and equity instruments, interest-rate and equity derivatives, non-trading loans, and long-term structured-note debt, driven by reduced observability and greater reliance on unobservable inputs.

nodes.title: Transfers between levels for instruments carried at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: The text reports recurring fair-value hierarchy transfers for 2021–2023, detailing amounts and causes, chiefly changes in input observability and significance; transfers are assumed at the quarter’s start. It summarizes 2021–2023 realized and unrealized gains and losses on fair-value assets and liabilities and their market-driven causes. It explains derivative CVA and FVA methodologies, key inputs, collateral treatment, and reported revenue impacts, and describes how own-credit DVA on fair-value-option liabilities is measured and reported in earnings or OCI.

Describes Level 3 valuation methods, judgment, significant unobservable inputs, disclosed ranges and averages, and their limitations, with a 2023 product and valuation-method table. Explains how yield and credit spreads, prepayments, defaults, loss severity, correlation, volatility, swaption values, interest-rate curves, and forward prices affect valuations and how their ranges are determined. Presents 2021–2023 Level 3 recurring fair-value rollforwards, hierarchy transfers, transfer drivers, and Level 3 asset analysis, including the 2023 balance and significant 2022 transfers. Summarizes realized and unrealized gains and losses and explains derivative CVA/FVA and own-credit DVA measurement and reporting.

nodes.title: Credit & funding adjustments & Assets and liabilities measured at FV on a nonrecurring basis
key_items: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.summary: Derivatives’ model-based fair values are adjusted for counterparty credit risk (CVA) and funding costs (FVA). CVA uses scenario-based exposures, default probabilities from CDS spreads, recovery estimates, and credit mitigants such as collateral and offset rights. FVA applies when market participants would price funding effects, using expected funding needs and market funding costs, including the Firm’s credit risk for liabilities; collateralized derivatives use OIS discounting and need no separate FVA. The text reports 2023–2021 CVA and FVA impacts on principal transactions revenue, excluding hedges. For fair-value-option liabilities, DVA reflects changes in default probability and loss given default estimated from bond credit spreads; realized gains or losses enter principal transactions revenue, while unrealized amounts enter OCI.

nodes.title: Assets and Liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents nonrecurring fair value measurements by product and hierarchy level at December 31, 2023 and 2022. In 2023, assets totaled $3.141 billion (including loans and other assets), all in Levels 2 and 3; there were no measured liabilities. In 2022, assets totaled $2.658 billion and liabilities $84 million. Other assets include equity-method investment impairments and equity securities valued using the measurement alternative; $412 million of 2023 Level 3 assets related to these securities. Reports annual nonrecurring fair value changes: losses of $1.065 billion in 2023 and $547 million in 2022, versus gains of $277 million in 2021. Other-asset results included measurement-alternative gains/(losses) of $(232) million, $(338) million, and $379 million, respectively; 2023 also included equity-method investment impairments. Refers readers to Note 12 for collateral-dependent loan valuation details.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.summary: The Firm uses the measurement alternative for certain equity securities lacking readily determinable fair values: cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes, with changes in other income and valuation adjustments as needed. At year-end 2023/2022, carrying values were $4.457/$4.096 billion; upward changes were $93/$488 million and downward changes or impairment were $(325)/$(826) million. Cumulative changes since 2018 were +$1.2 billion and −$1.2 billion. The balance includes about 37 million restricted Visa B shares, held at nominal value because conversion timing and rate are uncertain and their rights differ from Visa A shares. Derivatives tied to previously sold shares (23 million) retain conversion-rate risk, are valued using discounted cash flows, and recorded as trading liabilities, with fair-value changes in other income. In January 2024, Visa announced approved charter amendments and potential exchange offers that could permit staged transfers of some shares; timing and likelihood remain uncertain.

nodes.title: Estimated FV of financial instruments & Trading assets and liabilities
key_items: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
Financial instruments for which carrying value approximates fair value
nodes.summary: The notes describe the measurement alternative for equity securities without readily determinable fair values, including 2023–2022 carrying values and observable-price changes, and explain Visa B share restrictions, conversion uncertainty, related derivatives, and Visa’s proposed exchange program announced in January 2024. They also disclose estimated fair values and hierarchy classifications for financial instruments not carried at fair value, explain instruments whose carrying values approximate fair value and loan valuation methods, and present fair values of wholesale lending commitments, exclusions, and consumer commitment valuation limitations.

Explains JPMorgan Chase’s fair-value policies, governance, model approval, valuation adjustments, and U.S. GAAP hierarchy and methods across financial products. Presents 2023–2022 recurring and nonrecurring fair-value balances, hierarchy classifications, Level 3 inputs, rollforwards, transfers, gains and losses, and CVA, FVA, and DVA. Covers equity securities measured using the alternative method, including restricted Visa B shares and related derivatives, and estimated fair values and valuation methods for financial instruments, loans, and lending commitments not carried at fair value.

nodes.title: Note 3 - Fair value option
Note 3 - Fair value option (intro)
nodes.summary: The fair value option allows election of fair value for certain financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments. The Firm uses it to reduce income volatility from mismatched measurement bases and to reflect instruments managed at fair value. Elected instruments include certain loans and lending commitments, securities financing agreements, securitized interests with embedded credit derivatives, client-related structured notes and hybrid instruments, and certain long-term interests in CIB securitization trusts whose underlying assets are measured at fair value.

nodes.title: Changes in fair value under the fair value option election
nodes.summary: Presents 2021–2023 income-statement fair-value changes for instruments elected under the fair value option, excluding related risk-management instruments, with classifications and notes on OCI, income categories, interest and structured-note risk management. Explains how instrument-specific credit risk is measured for loans and commitments, long-term debt, and securities-financing agreements. Compares 2023 and 2022 aggregate fair value with remaining contractual principal for elected loans, long-term debt, and beneficial interests, including exclusions and principal-protection disclosures; also reports lending-related commitments and corresponding fair values.

nodes.title: Structured note products by balance sheet classification and risk component
nodes.summary: The table reports the fair value of structured notes by balance-sheet classification and primary risk exposure (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity) at December 31, 2023 and 2022. It includes amounts across short-term borrowings, deposits, and long-term debt, with total structured notes of $87.2 billion in 2023 and $105.0 billion in 2022. A footnote excludes deposits linked to precious metals for which the fair value option was not elected: $627 million in 2023 and $602 million in 2022.

Explains why the Firm elects the fair value option and identifies the types of instruments covered. Reports 2021–2023 fair-value changes and their income-statement classifications, related credit-risk measurement methods, and comparisons of fair value with remaining contractual principal for selected loans, debt, beneficial interests, and lending commitments. Also presents 2023 and 2022 structured-note fair values by balance-sheet classification and risk exposure, with an exclusion for certain precious-metal-linked deposits.

nodes.title: Note 4 - Credit risk concentrations
nodes.summary: Explains how JPMorgan Chase identifies and manages credit-risk concentrations: monitoring portfolios, obtaining collateral where permitted, senior-management oversight, consumer concentration management by product and U.S. region, and wholesale monitoring by industry and client. Wholesale risk-reduction methods include syndications, sales, securitizations, derivatives, netting and collateral. The Firm reports no significant concentration in any product or industry and considers loan terms and collateral in credit and allowance assessments. Tables show 2023 and 2022 on- and off-balance-sheet consumer and wholesale exposures by portfolio and industry, with notes on categories, exclusions, collateral, First Republic and PPP exposures, and related securities and cash.

nodes.title: Note 5 - Derivative instruments
Derivative Activities, Risk Management and Clearing
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives predominantly for client market-making and managing its own risks. Market-making derivatives help clients address interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity and commodity risks; the Firm offsets exposures with other derivatives or financial instruments. Risk-management derivatives address interest rate variability, foreign currency exposures and forecasted transactions, commodity inventory price changes, and counterparty credit risk, primarily through credit default swaps; related gains and losses are expected to substantially offset the managed risks. The Firm enters into bilateral OTC derivatives, exchange-traded contracts, and OTC-cleared contracts novated to central counterparties. It also clears client contracts as a clearing member but does not include those contracts in its consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Accounting for derivatives
Accounting for derivatives (intro)
nodes.summary: The Firm records all free-standing derivatives executed for its own account at fair value on the consolidated balance sheets. Under U.S. GAAP, it offsets derivative assets and liabilities and related cash collateral when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists. Derivative value changes are accounted for according to hedge designation and qualification; non-hedge derivatives are measured at fair value through earnings. Note disclosures provide details on derivative balances and gains and losses, while Notes 2 and 3 discuss embedded derivatives in structured notes.

nodes.title: Derivatives designated as hedges
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s hedge-accounting eligibility, documentation and effectiveness testing, quarterly review, and discontinuation rules; describes fair value, cash flow, and net investment hedges and their accounting, including the portfolio layer method adopted in 2023; and summarizes derivative uses, hedge designations or disclosure categories, and affected business segments for risk management, lending, market-making, and other activities.

nodes.title: Notional amount of derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s free-standing derivative notional amounts by contract type for 2023 and 2022, totaling $49.8 trillion and $49.5 trillion, respectively, and notes that notionals indicate activity but generally are not exchanged and greatly exceed potential losses. It also presents 2023 and 2022 derivative receivables and payables by contract type and hedge designation, showing gross and net balances on the consolidated balance sheets. Balances exclude certain structured notes; netting of derivatives and related collateral is applied where enforceable master netting agreements permit.

The section explains that free-standing derivatives are recorded at fair value, with assets, liabilities, and related collateral offset when enforceable master netting agreements allow; accounting for value changes depends on hedge designation, while non-hedges affect earnings. It covers hedge eligibility, documentation, effectiveness testing, review and discontinuation, fair value, cash flow, and net investment hedge accounting—including the portfolio layer method adopted in 2023—and derivatives’ risk-management and business uses. It reports 2023 and 2022 notionals by contract type, explains their limits as a measure of exposure, and presents gross and net receivables and payables by contract type and designation, with exclusions and netting qualifications.

nodes.title: Free-standing derivatives
key_items: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 and 2022 derivative receivables and payables on its consolidated balance sheets, by hedge designation and contract type, showing gross and net amounts. It explains balance-sheet netting under U.S. GAAP when enforceable master netting agreements are supported by legal opinions, and describes collateral eligible or ineligible for net presentation. Detailed tables compare gross, netted, and net receivables by contract and settlement type, including amounts with or without legal opinions and additional non-nettable collateral.

nodes.title: Derivatives netting and collateral
nodes.summary: The note explains derivative netting under master agreements when supported by legal opinions, and identifies additional collateral that mitigates counterparty risk but is not eligible for balance-sheet netting or table inclusion. It presents 2023 and 2022 gross, offset, and net derivative receivables and payables by contract type and settlement method, distinguishing balances with and without legal opinions, collateral not nettable, and final net amounts. Footnotes describe daily settlement of futures, collateral limits and eligibility, and cash collateral netted against derivatives.

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: Derivatives expose JPMorgan Chase to counterparty credit risk on receivables and liquidity risk on payables, which may require collateral or settlement after ratings downgrades. The Firm mitigates credit risk through enforceable netting and collateral agreements. Tables report downgrade-triggered net payables and collateral posted for 2023 and 2022, plus additional collateral and termination-settlement impacts under one- and two-notch downgrades; impacts generally arise only when ratings breach contract thresholds. The Firm may transfer assets while retaining exposure through derivatives; such transfers are usually accounted for as collateralized financings, and sale-accounted cases were immaterial in both years.

nodes.title: Derivatives designated as hedges
Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes derivative credit risk from counterparties failing to pay and its use of enforceable netting and collateral agreements to mitigate it, as well as liquidity risk from collateral requirements and downgrade-triggered terminations. At year-end 2023 and 2022, the note reports fair values of downgrade-triggered OTC and OTC-cleared net payables and collateral posted, plus estimated additional collateral and termination payments under one- and two-notch rating downgrades. It explains downgrade assumptions and table exclusions. Transfers made with matching derivatives are generally treated as collateralized financings; those qualifying as sales were immaterial in both years.

nodes.title: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
nodes.summary:
Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
The following tables provide information related to gains and losses recorded on derivatives based on their hedge accounting designation or purpose.

nodes.title: Fair value hedge gains and losses
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 fair value hedge gains and losses by interest-rate, foreign-exchange and commodity contract type, including derivative and hedged-item income effects, excluded-component amortization and fair-value changes, and OCI effects. Notes describe hedge exposures, income-statement classifications, excluded effectiveness components, and accounting methods. It also presents 2023 and 2022 carrying amounts and cumulative fair-value basis adjustments for AFS securities and long-term debt expected to affect future yields, with explanations of exclusions, portfolio-layer-method adoption, future income effects, and discontinued hedges.

nodes.title: Cash flow hedge gains and losses
nodes.summary: The text reports pre-tax gains and losses on interest-rate and foreign-exchange derivatives used in cash flow hedges for 2021–2023, including amounts recorded in OCI, changes in OCI, and amounts reclassified from AOCI to income. Interest-rate hedges primarily cover SOFR-indexed floating-rate assets, with results in net interest income; foreign-exchange hedges cover non-U.S.-dollar revenue and expenses, classified with the hedged items. No forecasted transactions failed. The Firm expects about $1.6 billion in after-tax AOCI net losses to enter income over the next 12 months; recognition periods extend up to six years for terminated hedges and seven years for open hedges, mainly covering core lending and borrowing.

nodes.title: Net investment hedge gains and losses
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 gains and losses on foreign-exchange derivatives in net investment hedges, with income and OCI amounts, and explains excluded hedge components and AOCI reclassifications. It summarizes income gains/losses on non-designated interest-rate, credit, and foreign-exchange derivatives used to manage specified mortgage, lending, and currency risks, including purposes and revenue categories. It describes derivatives used for market-making and other risks, then defines credit derivatives, outlines protection-buyer and seller risks, and explains JPMorgan’s market-making and risk-management uses.

Describes derivative credit and liquidity risks, mitigation through netting and collateral, downgrade-related collateral and termination exposure, and treatment of transfers. Reports income-statement effects of derivatives by hedge designation and purpose, including fair value, cash flow, and net investment hedges; related OCI, AOCI reclassifications, basis adjustments, accounting methods, exposures, and expected future income effects. Also covers non-designated derivatives used for risk management and market-making, including credit derivative purposes and risks.

nodes.title: Derivative Risk Management and Credit Derivatives
key_items: Risk management derivatives gains and losses
nodes.summary: Describes pre-tax gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management in 2021–2023, covering interest-rate, credit, and foreign-exchange contracts, their purposes, and income-statement locations. Explains derivatives used in market-making and to manage associated open-position and counterparty risks. Defines credit derivatives, outlines protection buyers’ and sellers’ risks, and describes the Firm’s roles as market-maker and end-user in managing customer needs and credit exposures.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management purposes
nodes.summary: The notes report pre-tax gains and losses on non-hedge-accounting derivatives used to manage specified risks in mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, MSRs, wholesale lending, and foreign-currency assets and liabilities. For 2023, 2022, and 2021, respectively, interest-rate derivatives recorded losses of $135 million, $827 million, and gains of $1,078 million; credit derivatives recorded losses of $441 million, gains of $51 million, and losses of $94 million; and foreign-exchange derivatives recorded losses of $2 million, $48 million, and gains of $94 million. Total results were losses of $578 million and $824 million, then gains of $1,078 million. Interest-rate results were predominantly recorded in mortgage fees and related income; credit and foreign-exchange results in principal transactions revenue. Credit derivatives address wholesale lending exposure, excluding counterparty-risk derivatives reported with market-making and other derivatives.

nodes.title: Gains and losses on derivatives related to market-making activities and other derivatives
nodes.summary: The Firm uses derivatives for market-making and to manage risks from net open positions, including counterparty credit risk; derivatives outside hedge-accounting and specified risk-management categories are included, with gains and losses primarily recorded in principal transactions revenue. Credit derivatives transfer third-party reference-entity credit risk from protection purchasers to sellers, who receive premiums but may owe payments after events such as bankruptcy, nonpayment, or restructuring. The Firm both buys and sells credit protection: as a market-maker to serve customers, and as an end-user to manage credit risks from lending, wholesale derivative counterparties, and certain market-making instruments.

nodes.title: Credit default swaps
nodes.summary: Credit default swaps (CDS) reference a single entity, an index or portfolio, and may be OTC or OTC-cleared. The Firm buys and sells single-name and index protection: single-name CDS address an entity’s default risk, while index CDS cover broader markets or segments. Indices contain multiple entities, are periodically refreshed, and remove entities after credit events. Tranche CDS provide customized portfolio-loss protection. Following a credit event, buyers claim from sellers—not reference entities—the difference between contract face value and the reference obligation’s recovery value; buyers need not own the underlying debt.

nodes.title: Credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Credit-related notes are funded derivatives in which investors pay par for credit protection on a reference entity or index and receive periodic credit-linked payments; par is repaid at maturity unless a specified credit event occurs, in which case settlement reflects the reference obligation’s recovery value, with no recourse to the defaulting entity. The text introduces year-end 2023 and 2022 tables of sold and purchased credit derivatives and notes. Protection sellers typically pay less than full notional after recovery. The Firm mitigates sold-protection risk with similar protection; other purchased protection includes related but nonidentical exposures, CIB credit-related notes, and protection for retained-portfolio loans. Notional is not the Firm’s primary risk measure because it omits event probability, recovery, and hedges.

nodes.title: Total credit derivatives and credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Reports credit derivative and credit-related note amounts (millions) for 2023 and 2022: protection sold, purchased protection on identical underlyings, resulting net protection sold/purchased, and other protection purchased. Defines other derivatives and notes, explains identical-underlying and settlement-value qualifications, and describes other purchased protection. It also introduces tables of protection-seller credit derivative notional amounts by reference-entity rating, remaining maturity, and total fair value; purchaser profiles are stated to be comparable.

nodes.title: Protection sold – credit derivatives ratings (a) /maturity profile December 31, 2023 (in millions)
nodes.summary: The table reports credit protection sold by reference-entity rating and maturity for December 31, 2023 and 2022, including investment-grade, noninvestment-grade, and total notionals for under one year, 1–5 years, and over five years, plus fair-value receivables, payables, and net fair value. Ratings are primarily based on S&P and Moody’s; fair values are gross before legally enforceable master netting agreements and cash collateral netting.

Covers derivative gains and losses for specified risk management, market-making, and other activities, including their accounting presentation and credit-risk uses. Explains credit protection, CDS structures and settlement, and funded credit-related notes. Reports sold and purchased protection, net exposures, hedging and risk-measure limitations, and protection sold by rating and maturity, with fair values and related qualifications.

Explains JPMorgan Chase’s derivative activities for client market-making and risk management, contract types and clearing, and accounting for free-standing derivatives and fair value, cash flow, net investment, and portfolio-layer hedges. Presents notionals, receivables and payables, balance-sheet netting, collateral and settlement details, and related gains, losses, OCI and AOCI effects. Covers counterparty credit and liquidity risks, downgrade-triggered collateral and termination exposures, asset transfers, and credit derivatives, including CDS, protection bought and sold, net exposures, ratings, maturities, fair values, and risk-measure limitations.

nodes.title: Note 6 - Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense
Investment banking fees
nodes.summary: The note explains noninterest revenue from customer contracts, including demand-terminable arrangements and fixed-term obligations whose revenue depends on future events or asset values. It describes investment banking underwriting, loan arrangement/syndication, and advisory fees, their recognition, and reported fees for 2021–2023, earned primarily by CIB. It also explains principal transactions revenue drivers, realized and unrealized gains and losses, client market-making in financial and physical commodities, hedge and risk-management derivatives, and the scope and presentation limits of the related trading-revenue table.

nodes.title: Principal transactions
nodes.summary: Note 6 explains customer-contract noninterest revenue recognition: on-demand services are generally complete when provided, while fixed-term future obligations tied to uncertain events or asset values are recognized when outcomes are known. It covers investment banking underwriting and advisory fees, their recognition and 2021–2023 amounts; principal-transaction drivers, trading instruments, derivatives, commodity activities, exclusions, and revenue by instrument and year; lending- and deposit-fee types, recognition, amounts, and First Republic discount amortization; asset-management fee types, recognition, amounts, and First Republic impact; and brokerage, custody, administration, and other commissions and their recognition and net presentation of certain costs. It identifies the primary business segments earning these fees.

nodes.title: Lending- and deposit-related fees
nodes.summary: The notes report principal transactions revenue by trading instrument for 2021–2023, including private equity losses and valuation-adjustment and held-for-sale-position disclosures; revenue is earned primarily by CIB. They describe lending- and deposit-related fee sources, recognition over service periods, segment earners, and annual totals, including the First Republic commitment-discount amortization. They also explain asset management fee types and recognition policies, provide 2021–2023 totals and First Republic disclosure, and identify AWM and CCB as the primary earners.

nodes.title: Commissions and other fees
nodes.summary: Commissions and other fees include brokerage and custody-related services and other products. Brokerage commissions are recognized when client trades occur, net of certain clearing-house and exchange costs; administration fees for custody, fund services, securities lending, and clearance are recognized as services are provided. Other fees, including travel and annuity sales commissions, depositary receipt services, and other service fees, are recognized when rendered. Revenue totaled $6.836 billion in 2023, $6.581 billion in 2022, and $6.624 billion in 2021, with brokerage commissions, administration fees, and other fees reported separately. These fees are earned primarily by CIB, CCB, and AWM.

nodes.title: Mortgage fees and related income
nodes.summary: Mortgage fees and related income comprise CCB mortgage production revenue—including origination, pipeline risk management, loan-sale gains/losses and fair-value adjustments—and servicing revenue from third-party loans, MSR valuation and hedging, excess-servicing securitizations, and certain repurchased government-insured loans; mortgage-loan interest is reported as interest income (see Note 15). Card income includes transaction interchange and merchant processing, deferred origination costs and annual fees, and proprietary reward costs recorded as reductions. Co-brand partner payments are classified as marketing expense, reductions of card income, or deferred origination costs according to their purpose. Card income for 2023, 2022, and 2021 was $4.784 billion, $4.420 billion, and $5.102 billion, respectively, with components shown for interchange/processing, rewards and partner payments, and other income. Card income is earned primarily by CCB, CIB, and CB.

nodes.title: Card income
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 commissions and other fees by brokerage, administration, and other fees, noting other fees include travel and annuity commissions and service fees recognized as services are rendered; revenue is earned mainly by CIB, CCB, and AWM. It explains mortgage fee and income components, including loan production, servicing, fair-value and risk-management effects, securitizations, and where mortgage interest income is recorded. It describes card income, recognition of transaction income and fees, reward costs, and co-brand partner agreements and payment accounting. A table presents card income components for 2021–2023, with a note on deferred origination costs and annual-fee amortization; card income is earned mainly by CCB, CIB, and CB.

nodes.title: Other income
nodes.summary: The text details other income for 2021–2023, including operating lease income, tax-oriented investment losses (offset by related tax credits), and acquisition- or investment-related gains, with references to supporting notes. It summarizes other expenses—legal, FDIC-related, and First Republic-related—and explains the FDIC’s November 2023 special assessment: a quarterly 3.36-basis-point charge on qualifying institutions to replenish the Deposit Insurance Fund, resulting in the Firm recognizing an estimated $2.9 billion pretax expense in Q4 2023. Segment details are referenced in Note 32.

Explains recognition policies, sources, business-segment earners, and 2021–2023 amounts for customer-contract noninterest revenue: investment banking and principal transactions, lending and deposit fees, asset management, commissions and other fees, mortgage income, and card income. Covers trading instruments, gains and losses, derivatives, commodities, valuation adjustments, First Republic-related effects, mortgage production and servicing, card rewards and partner payments, and revenue presentation. Also details other income, including lease income, tax-oriented investment losses and acquisition or investment gains, and other expenses, including legal, FDIC-related and First Republic costs and the 2023 FDIC special assessment.

nodes.title: Note 7 - Interest income and Interest expense
nodes.summary: Note 7 explains that interest income and expense are recorded in the consolidated income statements according to the underlying asset or liability. For fair-value instruments, interest accruals are generally included, while derivatives and instruments with embedded derivatives that would be separately accounted for under U.S. GAAP absent the fair value option report fair-value changes, including interest, primarily in principal transactions revenue. Loan and securities interest includes premium/discount amortization or accretion and deferred loan fees and costs, recognized on a level-yield basis; related accounting details are cross-referenced to Notes 10, 11, 12, and 20. A table reports 2021–2023 interest income by asset category, interest expense by liability category, net interest income, credit-loss provision, and net interest income after provision. Footnotes identify tax-exempt securities, explain negative securities-borrowing interest, specify brokerage-related receivables and payables, and note First Republic acquisition discount accretion.

nodes.title: Note 8 - Pension and other postretirement employee benefit plans
Gains and losses
key_items: Note 8 – Pension and other postretirement employee benefit plans
nodes.summary: The note describes JPMorgan Chase’s U.S. and international defined benefit pension, OPEB, and defined contribution plans, including the closure and freezing of its principal U.S. pension plan and 401(k) contributions. It reports 2023–2022 obligations, assets, funded status, AOCI, discount rates, and annual pension/OPEB and defined contribution costs. It explains OCI gains and losses, amortization, and the 2022 pension settlement remeasurement; actuarial assumptions and their basis; investment strategy, allocation ranges, and affiliate exposures; and fair-value measurement methods and asset totals by hierarchy level.

nodes.title: Pension and OPEB Assumptions and Investments
nodes.summary: The page reports 2021–2023 actuarial discount rates and expected asset returns for defined benefit pension and OPEB plans. It explains how expected returns and discount rates are determined, describes portfolio diversification and allocation reviews, and lists 2023 allocation ranges for the principal pension plan. It also notes restrictions on direct investment in JPMorgan Chase securities and affiliate-managed plan investments of $1.8 billion in 2023 and $1.7 billion in 2022.

nodes.title: Fair value measurement of the plans’ assets and liabilities
key_items: Plan assumptions; Investment strategy and asset allocation
Pension plan assets and liabilities measured at fair value
nodes.summary: The note presents fair value measurements of defined benefit pension and OPEB plan assets and liabilities at December 31, 2023 and 2022, referring readers to Note 2 for fair value hierarchy levels and valuation methods. It reports assets by Levels 1–3 and assets measured using NAV as a practical expedient, net pension plan payables, and total plan asset fair value. Level 1 assets are mainly equity securities, government debt, and cash equivalents; Level 2 mainly corporate and government debt; Level 3 comprises corporate-owned life insurance, fund investments, and participating annuity contracts in 2023, and insurance policies and annuities in 2022.

nodes.title: Note 10 - Investment securities
Note 10 - Investment securities (intro)

nodes.title: AFS securities impairment
nodes.summary: Presents 2023 and 2022 fair values and gross unrealized losses for impaired AFS securities by aging and type, excluding U.S.-guaranteed securities whose losses primarily reflect interest rates; notes the First Republic impact. nodes.title: Investment Securities Credit Risk and Allowances
key_items: Allowance for credit losses on investment securities
nodes.summary: Explains when AFS impairment is recognized in earnings, as a credit-loss allowance, or in OCI; outlines credit-loss factors and securitization cash-flow assessments. HTM allowances cover expected lifetime losses, using statistical PD/LGD methods for municipal and commercial mortgage-backed securities and discounted expected cash flows for CLOs and residential mortgage-backed securities, with significant management judgment. nodes.summary: Reports selected impacts of investment securities on income for 2021–2023, including realized gains and losses, investment securities losses, and credit-loss provisions. Notes explain yield methodology, exclusions for credit-loss allowances and hedge adjustments, mortgage securities’ contractual versus estimated lives, and First Republic-related securities.

Covers AFS and HTM accounting, portfolio-layer hedge adoption and transfers, portfolio composition, fair values, amortized costs, unrealized gains and losses, purchases, accrued interest, basis adjustments, and credit quality and reviews. Describes AFS impairment recognition and credit assessment, HTM lifetime-loss allowance methods and assumptions, and allowance balances and adjustments. Reports impaired securities by type and aging, First Republic impacts, annual realized gains and losses and credit provisions, and 2023 securities by category and contractual maturity with yields and related methodology.

nodes.title: Note 11 - Securities financing activities
key_items: Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes securities financing agreements, their purposes, balance-sheet and income-statement treatment, fair-value elections, and the absence of credit-loss allowances for resale and securities-borrowed arrangements in 2022–2023. It outlines collateral, margin, monitoring, possession, and netting practices for managing credit and liquidity risk. Tables detail gross, netted, non-nettable and net balances by agreement type and year, collateral asset types, and remaining maturities. The note also explains securities received in lending transactions and transfers that failed sale accounting and were recorded as collateralized financings.

nodes.title: Note 12 - Loans
Loan accounting framework
key_items: Interest income; Allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The note explains loan accounting by strategy: held-for-investment, held-for-sale, or fair value. Held-for-investment loans are carried at amortized cost, with rules for interest accrual, fee and premium amortization, past-due and nonaccrual status, interest reversal or cash/cost-recovery recognition, and return to accrual; credit cards generally remain accruing until paid or charged off. It describes the expected-loss allowance and its income-statement effect, consumer and wholesale charge-off triggers, government-guaranteed exceptions, and collateral valuation methods and updates. Held-for-sale loans use lower of cost or fair value, with valuation changes in noninterest revenue and deferred fees affecting basis; they remain subject to nonaccrual rules but not allowance or charge-off policies. Fair-value-option loans record fair-value changes and upfront fees in noninterest revenue, costs as incurred, accrue contractual interest, and likewise follow nonaccrual but not allowance or charge-off policies; related disclosures are referenced.

nodes.title: Loan classification changes
nodes.summary: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value, with credit losses charged to the allowance and non-credit losses recognized in noninterest revenue; loans moved back are recorded at amortized cost and assessed for impairment. The Firm modifies loans for borrowers in financial difficulty to reduce losses, offering concessions such as rate reductions, term extensions, payment delays, or principal forgiveness. Since January 1, 2023, these modifications are accounted for as FDMs rather than TDRs. Non-credit-card FDMs are generally nonaccrual until at least six months or six payments of performance and repayment is reasonably assured, with limited exceptions for current loans. FDM allowances reflect expected redefaults. Before 2023, qualifying concessions were TDRs, generally assessed using asset-specific allowances that remained applicable for the loan’s life; insignificant, non-concession modifications were excluded.

nodes.title: Foreclosed property
nodes.summary: The Firm acquires real, commercial, and personal property through loan restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures, recognizing it when received in satisfaction of a loan. Real estate is generally recognized at foreclosure sale or when a deed in lieu is executed. Foreclosed assets are reported in other assets, initially at fair value less estimated selling costs, and reviewed quarterly, with carrying value adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value. Subsequent fair-value changes affect noninterest revenue; property operating costs are charged to other expense.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.summary: The Firm groups loans into Consumer excluding credit card, Credit card, and Wholesale segments, with risk monitored by loan classes: residential real estate, auto and other, credit card, and wholesale loans secured by real estate, commercial and industrial, or other. Notes define included businesses, borrowers, collateral, and methodologies. Tables report retained, held-for-sale, and fair-value balances by segment for 2023 and 2022, with notes on First Republic loans, accrued interest, and discounts and fees. Additional tables show retained-loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale for both years; later sales of reclassified loans are excluded from sales.

nodes.title: Credit card
key_items: Gains and losses on sales of loans
nodes.summary: The notes describe the Firm’s three loan portfolio segments—Consumer excluding credit card, Credit card, and Wholesale—and the loan classes and risk-monitoring scope within each. They present 2023 and 2022 balances by segment and accounting treatment, with First Republic, accrued-interest, and carrying-value footnotes. Tables report retained-loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale for 2021–2023, including related exclusions and acquisition details. The text also reports annual gains or losses on loan and lending-commitment sales and notes that sales can affect credit-loss provisions.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards primarily comprise scored residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines, auto, and business banking loans, focused on prime borrowers. They include junior-lien home equity loans, interest-only mortgages, and payment-option loans that may negatively amortize. Retained balances were $397.3 billion in 2023 ($326.4 billion residential real estate; $70.9 billion auto and other), versus $300.8 billion in 2022; 2023 residential loans included $90.7 billion associated with First Republic. Delinquency rates are the main credit indicator: 30-plus-day delinquencies provide early warning, while residential delinquencies over 150 days strongly indicate likely foreclosure or liquidation. Residential risk is also assessed using current or combined LTV, collateral geography, and refreshed FICO scores; high LTV and low FICO together indicate greater default risk. For scored auto and business banking loans, geographic distribution reflects regional economic conditions and events affecting performance.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.summary: The text reports retained residential mortgage credit quality for 2023 and 2022, including delinquency and gross charge-offs by origination year and revolving-loan status, with definitions and exclusions. It describes lien composition, higher delinquency among revolving loans converted to term loans, nonaccrual balances, LTV/FICO indicators, geographic concentrations, and related methodologies and First Republic amounts. It summarizes 2023 financial-difficulty modifications (FDMs), their effects, past-due and redefault balances, and trial and Chapter 7 loans; compares 2022–2021 TDR volumes, concession types, modification effects and redefaults; and gives balances in active or suspended foreclosure.

nodes.title: Residential Loan Modifications, TDRs, and Defaults
key_items: Financial effects of TDRs and redefaults
nodes.summary: The page describes residential loan modifications for financially distressed borrowers: FDM definitions effective in 2023, their $136 million volume, effects on loan life and interest rates, and past-due and redefault amounts; it also notes trial modifications and Chapter 7 loans. For 2022–2021, it explains TDR criteria, volumes, modification counts and concession types, then reports permanent-modification effects—including rates, terms, charge-offs, principal changes, and one-year redefaults—with table scope and caveats.

nodes.title: Active and suspended foreclosure
nodes.summary: The text reports residential mortgages in active or suspended foreclosure outside REO ($566 million in 2023; $565 million in 2022). For retained auto and other loans, it presents 2023 and 2022 delinquency and gross charge-offs by origination year and loan type, including 30-plus-day delinquency ratios; PPP loans backed by the SBA are excluded from certain measures. It also reports nonaccrual balances and loan geographic distribution, with notes on SBA-guaranteed loans, collateral-dependent charge-downs, and cash-basis interest. Finally, auto and other financial-difficulty modifications were immaterial in 2023, as were TDRs in 2022 and 2021.

Covers consumer loans excluding credit cards, their composition, prime-borrower focus, retained balances, and credit-risk measures. Reports residential mortgage delinquency, charge-offs, liens, nonaccruals, LTV/FICO and geographic risk, First Republic balances, modifications for financially distressed borrowers, prior-year TDRs and redefaults, and foreclosure balances. Also presents auto and other loan delinquency, charge-offs, nonaccruals, geographic distribution, measurement exclusions and methodologies, and notes that related modifications and TDRs were immaterial.

nodes.title: Credit card loan portfolio
Credit card loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: The credit card portfolio comprises loans originated and purchased by the Firm. Delinquency at 30 days is the primary early-warning credit-quality measure, with 90-day delinquency, geographic distribution, and delinquency and gross charge-off data also considered. Credit scores offer general trend insight but are lagging and incomplete; quarterly refreshed FICO scores from a random sample are reported, and FICO is the industry benchmark. The Firm generally originates to prime borrowers, though scores may later decline. Tables compare 2023 and 2022 retained-loan balances by revolving versus converted-to-term status, delinquency categories and ratios, and gross charge-offs.

nodes.title: Other credit quality indicators
nodes.summary: The text reports retained credit card loan balances by geography for 2023 and 2022, with regions ranked by 2023 balances, and refreshed FICO distribution: 85.8% at least 660, 14.0% below 660, and 0.2% unavailable in 2023, versus 86.8%, 13.0%, and 0.2% in 2022. It explains financial-difficulty modifications (FDMs), typically 60-month fixed-payment plans with reduced interest; missed payments continue aging toward standard charge-off, and credit lines are usually not reinstated. In 2023, FDMs totaled $648 million (0.31% of retained loans), involving term extensions and rate reductions from a weighted average 23.19% to 3.64%; another $27 million underwent trial modifications, which are not FDMs. FDM payment status totaled $648 million: $558 million current or under 30 days past due, $59 million 30–89 days past due, and $31 million 90 or more days past due. Re-defaults totaled $50 million; default means two consecutive missed payments, and modified loans remain in the program and follow standard charge-off policy.

nodes.title: Financial effects of TDRs and redefaults
nodes.summary: Before 2023, credit card loans modified with concessions for financially distressed borrowers were generally reported as TDRs, chiefly under long-term programs with fixed payments (usually 60 months) and reduced interest rates; insignificant or non-concession modifications were excluded. For 2022 and 2021, new TDR balances were $418 million and $393 million, with weighted-average interest rates falling from 19.86% to 4.13% and 17.75% to 5.14%, respectively; redefaults within one year were $34 million and $57 million. New enrollments were under 1% of retained card loans. Redefault meant missing two consecutive payments; loans stayed in the program and were charged off under standard policy. Notes define balances as pre-modification and redefaults as balances at quarter-end of default.

Describes the Firm’s originated and purchased credit card portfolio, including early-warning delinquency measures, the limitations and quarterly sample-based use of FICO scores, and comparisons of 2023 and 2022 retained balances, revolving and term loans, delinquency, charge-offs, geographic distribution, and credit-score bands. Explains financial-difficulty modifications, their terms, balances, payment status, trial modifications, redefaults, and charge-off treatment. Also gives 2021–2022 TDR balances, interest-rate reductions, redefaults, enrollment levels, and definitions of reported balances and default.

nodes.title: Wholesale loan portfolio
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale loan portfolio, internal risk ratings based on probability of default and loss given default, rating factors and review, investment-grade and criticized classifications, and industry diversification. It presents 2023 and 2022 loan balances, ratings, charge-offs, origination-year and revolving-loan breakdowns by real estate, commercial and industrial, and other classes; real-estate subcategories; geographic distribution, delinquency and nonaccrual status. It also details 2023 financial-difficulty modifications, their terms and payment status, redefaults and unfunded commitments, and describes pre-2023 troubled debt restructurings and comparative volumes.

Explains loan accounting under held-for-investment, held-for-sale, and fair-value methods, including interest recognition, credit-loss allowances, charge-offs, collateral valuation, classification transfers, and current and pre-2023 borrower modifications. Covers foreclosed-property recognition and measurement; portfolio segments, loan classes, balances, purchases, sales, and reclassifications; and consumer, credit-card, and wholesale portfolio composition and credit-risk measures. Reports delinquencies, nonaccruals, charge-offs, risk ratings, collateral, geographic and industry exposure, financially distressed modifications, redefaults, and prior troubled debt restructurings.

nodes.title: Note 13 - Allowance for credit losses
Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lendingrelated commitments
nodes.summary: The note explains the allowance for credit losses, its components, income-statement treatment, quarterly review, and significant estimation uncertainty. It describes lifetime-loss methods for retained loans and noncancellable commitments, expected-life and accrued-interest policies, and collective versus individual assessments and relevant consumer and wholesale risk factors. Portfolio estimates use five macroeconomic scenarios over an eight-quarter forecast, followed by reversion to historical losses, with management adjustments for qualitative risks. Individual assessments cover collateral-dependent and nonaccrual loans; 2023 troubled-debt guidance adoption changed modified-loan methods and reduced the allowance by $587 million, increasing after-tax retained earnings by $446 million. The note also covers collateral and discounted-cash-flow measurement, modified-loan estimates, and allowances for other amortized-cost assets, including collateral-mitigated lending exposures.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses and related information
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.summary: The tables detail JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 allowance for loan losses, lending-related commitments and investment securities, charge-offs and recoveries, provisions, balances, and asset-specific versus portfolio-based impairment across consumer, card, and wholesale portfolios, including related loan and commitment balances. Notes explain accounting adoption effects, CIB receivables, First Republic, collateral-dependent loans, balance-sheet presentation, and commitments excluded from allowances. The discussion explains the 2023 $3.1 billion net allowance increase, its consumer and wholesale drivers, First Republic reserve, macroeconomic scenario updates, and $587 million reduction from TDR guidance adoption. It describes the five-scenario estimation method, adverse-case unemployment and GDP projections, 2022–2023 central-case forecasts, future estimate updates, and references for further credit-risk information.

Explains allowance-for-credit-loss methodology, components, income-statement treatment, quarterly review, estimation uncertainty, expected-life policies, and collective and individual assessments for loans, commitments, securities, and other amortized-cost assets. Covers macroeconomic scenarios, qualitative adjustments, collateral and cash-flow valuation, modified-loan accounting, and the 2023 adoption of troubled-debt guidance. Tables present 2021–2023 allowances, balances, provisions, charge-offs, recoveries, and impairment by portfolio; accompanying notes discuss accounting effects, First Republic, exclusions, and drivers of the 2023 $3.1 billion net allowance increase, including forecasts and risk factors.

nodes.title: Note 14 - Variable interest entities
Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs
Credit card securitizations
nodes.summary: Note 14 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s VIE consolidation policies and defines Firm-sponsored VIEs, then lists major sponsored structures by business segment, activity, and 10-K page reference. It describes other segments’ VIE involvement and consolidation or exposure practices, including AWM funds, CB lending, Corporate investments, and CIB third-party-sponsored VIEs. nodes.title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
key_items: Residential mortgage; Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s sponsored mortgage, commercial mortgage and consumer-loan securitizations, including servicing, retained interests, consolidation criteria and maximum exposure to loss. It explains residential and commercial securitization roles, re-securitizations and shared decision-making, reports securities transferred to agency re-securitizations in 2021–2023 and interests in nonconsolidated VIEs, and notes that no agency or private-label re-securitization VIEs were consolidated.

nodes.title: Multi-seller conduits
nodes.summary: The text describes Firm-administered multi-seller conduits: their receivables-backed, commercial-paper funding; seller-provided credit enhancements; JPMorgan Chase Bank liquidity and program-wide credit support; the Firm’s consolidation rationale, roles, exposures, commercial-paper holdings, lack of a general purchase obligation, and outstanding off-balance-sheet commitments.
