nodes.title: Municipal bond vehicles
nodes.summary: The notes report interests in nonconsolidated re-securitization VIEs of $3.371 billion in 2023 versus $2.580 billion in 2022, with no U.S. government or Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs consolidated. They describe multi-seller conduits’ financing, credit and liquidity support, consolidation rationale, commercial paper holdings, and unfunded client commitments. They also explain municipal bond/tender option trusts, floater and residual securities, customer versus Firm-sponsored structures, Firm service-provider roles, and limits and conditions on liquidity-provider exposure.

Reviews JPMorgan Chase’s significant sponsored VIEs, consolidation policies, activities, and exposures across business segments. Covers credit card trusts, servicing, retained interests, consolidation, asset limits, and year-end interests; mortgage, commercial mortgage, consumer-loan, and re-securitization trusts, including interests, risks, ratings, and consolidation status; multi-seller conduits, their funding, credit and liquidity support, exposures, and commitments; and municipal bond/tender-option trusts, their structures, Firm roles, holdings, and limits on liquidity obligations.

nodes.title: Consolidated VIE assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: Presents consolidated VIE assets and liabilities by program type for 2023 and 2022, including firm-sponsored credit card trusts, multi-seller conduits, municipal bond vehicles, mortgage securitization entities, and other VIEs. It explains why the Firm consolidates non-customer tender-option bond trusts and describes their liquidity arrangements. Notes clarify asset and liability classifications, settlement and recourse, long-term beneficial interests, residential mortgage securitizations, and assets included in the “Other” and CIB categories.

nodes.title: VIEs sponsored by third parties
key_items: Tax credit vehicles; Customer municipal bond vehicles (TOB trusts)
nodes.summary: The Firm transacts at arm’s length with third-party-sponsored VIEs in roles such as derivative counterparty, liquidity provider, investor, underwriter, agent, trustee, or custodian. It generally does not consolidate VIEs when it lacks significant decision-making power or potentially significant variable interests, reporting positions like other third-party transactions. It also invests as a limited partner in unconsolidated tax-credit vehicles controlled by third-party managers, earning mainly tax credits. Maximum loss exposure was $35.1 billion in 2023 ($14.7 billion unfunded) and $30.2 billion in 2022 ($10.6 billion unfunded); capital may be withheld pending project qualification. For customer municipal bond TOB trusts, the Firm may provide remarketing, liquidity, or tender-option services; certain liquidity agreements provide recourse to residual holders for termination shortfalls, without intent to shield them from bond losses. The Firm does not consolidate these trusts. Maximum liquidity exposure was $5.1 billion in 2023 and $5.8 billion in 2022; VIE assets were $7.3 billion and $8.2 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Loan securitizations
nodes.summary: The Firm securitizes and sells residential and commercial mortgages, credit card receivables, and other consumer loans to meet investor demand and generate liquidity. When it need not consolidate the trust, it records a transfer as a sale only if the assets are legally isolated from its creditors, the transferee can pledge or exchange them, and the Firm lacks effective control. For qualifying sales, it recognizes a gain or loss based on proceeds received—including cash, beneficial interests, and servicing assets—versus the assets’ carrying value; gains and losses are reported as noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Securitization activity
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 securitization activity for nonconsolidated, Firm-sponsored entities with sale accounting, including principal securitized, cash flows, and assumptions for valuing retained residential and commercial mortgage interests; it notes exclusions and asset classifications. It describes nonrecourse mortgage-loan and excess-MSR sales, GSE and Ginnie Mae guarantees, nonconsolidation, limited credit-risk sharing, and related disclosures. Tables summarize loan-sale carrying values, cash or securities proceeds, and gains or losses. It also explains options to repurchase delinquent government-backed loans and reports repurchased or eligible loans, real estate owned, and foreclosed guaranteed mortgages for 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: Loan delinquencies and liquidation losses
nodes.summary: The table reports components, delinquencies, and net liquidation losses or recoveries for loans in Firm-sponsored private-label securitization entities where JPMorgan Chase retained continuing involvement, as of or for the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2022. It covers residential mortgage (prime/Alt-A and option ARMs; subprime), commercial and other loans, total securitized loans and assets, amounts 90 days past due, and net liquidation losses or recoveries, in millions.

Reviews JPMorgan Chase’s sponsored and third-party variable interest entities (VIEs), including their activities, consolidation policies, assets, liabilities, retained interests, risks, exposures, support, and commitments across credit card, mortgage, consumer-loan, conduit, municipal bond, and other structures. Covers third-party VIE investments and maximum loss exposures; loan securitization accounting and sale criteria; 2021–2023 securitization activity, proceeds, gains or losses, retained-interest valuation, guarantees, repurchases, and foreclosures; and 2022–2023 delinquencies and liquidation losses or recoveries for securitized loans.

nodes.title: Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets
Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets (intro)
nodes.summary: Goodwill is established in acquisitions as purchase price less acquired net asset fair value, subject to one-year measurement-period adjustments; it is not amortized and is allocated to reporting units, with annual or event-driven impairment testing. Tables show segment goodwill and 2021–2023 changes, including acquisition-related additions and foreign-exchange effects. No impairment occurred in those years. Testing compares reporting-unit fair value with carrying value, using allocated capital as a proxy and discounted cash-flow valuations, checked against comparable-company data and Firm market capitalization. Future business, economic, regulatory, or valuation deterioration could cause material impairment.

nodes.title: Mortgage servicing rights
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s mortgage servicing rights (MSRs): their cash-flow basis, recognition, fair-value election, aggregate classification, OAS valuation model, inputs, and interest-rate sensitivity. It describes hedging MSR value changes with derivatives and securities, then presents 2021–2023 MSR activity, valuation drivers, servicing income, serviced-loan balances, and servicer advances, including purchase/disposition details and advance recoverability. It also reports mortgage fees and risk-management results and gives 2022–2023 fair-value sensitivities to adverse changes in prepayment speeds and option-adjusted spreads, noting assumptions interact and sensitivities are not directly extrapolatable.

nodes.title: Other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Other intangible assets are initially recorded at fair value, mainly in business combinations. Finite-lived assets, including core deposit and customer relationship intangibles, are amortized over their expected-benefit-based useful lives; indefinite-lived assets, such as asset management contracts, are not amortized. At year-end 2023 versus 2022, gross carrying values were $4.2 billion versus $1.9 billion, accumulated amortization $994 million versus $679 million, and net finite-lived and indefinite-lived values $2.0 billion and $1.2 billion versus $707 million and $517 million. 2023 assets included First Republic-related intangibles and CIFM contracts. Amortization expense was $315 million in 2023 and $145 million in 2022; estimated future expense for 2024–2028 is $330 million, $294 million, $290 million, $288 million, and $272 million. Assets are tested annually or when impairment indicators arise; impairment is recorded in other expense.

The section covers goodwill recognition, allocation, annual or event-driven impairment testing, 2021–2023 balances and changes, and the absence of impairment, while noting potential future risks. It explains mortgage servicing rights accounting, valuation and assumptions, hedging, activity and valuation drivers, servicing income, loan balances, advances, fees, risk-management results, and fair-value sensitivities. It also describes other intangible assets’ recognition, finite- and indefinite-lived treatment, 2022–2023 balances, First Republic-related additions, amortization expense and forecasts, and impairment testing.

nodes.title: Note 16 - Premises and equipment
nodes.summary: Premises and equipment comprises land at cost; buildings, leasehold improvements, internal-use software, and furniture and equipment at cost less depreciation or amortization; and operating lease right-of-use assets. Totaled $30.157 billion at December 31, 2023, versus $27.734 billion in 2022, with amounts detailed for land/buildings/leasehold improvements, right-of-use assets, and other equipment/software. Some right-of-use assets are reported in Other assets. Depreciation and amortization use straight-line methods; leasehold improvements are depreciated over the shorter of remaining lease term or useful life. Software development costs are capitalized and amortized once ready for use. Useful lives are 10–50 years for buildings and improvements and 3–10 years for software and equipment. Impairment is assessed when circumstances suggest an asset may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: Note 17 - Deposits
nodes.summary: Note 17 reports deposits at December 31, 2023 and 2022 by U.S. and non-U.S. offices and by noninterest-bearing versus interest-bearing status, including amounts measured at fair value under the elected fair value option for structured notes. It also gives time deposits at or above insured limits by office location, noting all non-U.S. time deposits typically exceed those limits, and the 2023 remaining maturities of interest-bearing time deposits by year and office location.

nodes.title: Note 18 - Leases
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 lease note describes its lessee accounting and operating-lease portfolio: terms, options, component elections, liability and right-of-use asset measurement, expenses, cash flows, balances, discount rates, future payments, and signed leases not yet commenced. It also covers its lessor auto and equipment financing, asset depreciation and income recognition, impairment and residual-value risk management, leased-asset carrying values, historical lease income and depreciation, and future lease receipts.

nodes.title: Note 19 - Accounts payable and other liabilities
nodes.summary: Accounts payable and other liabilities include brokerage payables to customers and for unsettled security purchases, plus accrued expenses such as compensation, credit card rewards, operating leases, interest, merchant servicing, income taxes, and litigation reserves. Total liabilities were $290.3 billion in 2023 versus $300.1 billion in 2022; brokerage payables were $162.0 billion and $188.7 billion, while other liabilities were $128.3 billion and $111.4 billion. Credit card rewards liabilities were $13.2 billion and $11.3 billion, respectively. These liabilities reflect expected redemption costs, accrue as rewards are earned, decline upon redemption, and depend on redemption-rate and per-point-cost assumptions; current-period effects are recognized in Card Income. Related notes cover interest, leases, taxes, and litigation.

nodes.title: Note 20 - Long-term debt
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s long-term debt is issued in multiple currencies, mainly U.S. dollars, at fixed and variable rates; certain indexed instruments are carried at fair value, with valuation changes generally in principal transactions revenue and DVA-related unrealized changes in OCI. The maturity table reports 2023 and 2022 carrying values by parent/subsidiary debt type, remaining term, rates, and beneficial interests. Notes detail First Republic-related purchase notes and FHLB advances, secured and fair-value debt, zero-coupon notes, beneficial-interest exclusions, rate methodology, callable debt, and annual maturities through 2028. Weighted-average rates were 3.65%/3.26% before derivatives and 5.20%/4.89% after derivatives for 2023/2022. Subsidiary debt guarantees rose to $41.1 billion from $28.2 billion; unsecured debt has no specified rating- or performance-triggered acceleration, borrowing restrictions, or collateral requirements.

nodes.title: Note 21 - Preferred stock
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s preferred-stock note describes its authorization of 200 million $1-par shares and their priority over common stock in liquidation. It tabulates outstanding non-cumulative series for 2023 and 2022, shares, carrying values, issue and redemption dates, fixed or floating rates, and 2021–2023 dividends. Footnotes explain depositary shares, SOFR/CMT benchmarks, conversion and payment terms, prorated initial dividends, and rate changes. Each share has $10,000 liquidation value and redemption price; aggregate liquidation value was $27.7 billion at year-end 2023. The firm redeemed Series I, V, and Z in 2022. Series may be redeemed on eligible dividend dates or after a capital-treatment event, subject to Federal Reserve non-objection.

nodes.title: Note 22 - Common stock
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase was authorized to issue 9.0 billion $1-par common shares at year-end 2023 and 2022. The note details 2021–2023 issued, treasury, reissued, and outstanding share balances, repurchases (69.5, 23.1, and 119.7 million shares; costing $9.898 billion, $3.122 billion, and $18.448 billion), and related tax and regulatory context, including the 2022 temporary pause. A May 2022 board authorization permits up to $30 billion in repurchases. Management controls timing and method, subject to market, legal, regulatory, capital, and investment factors; the program has no price targets or timetable and may be suspended. About 61.6 million shares were reserved for employee and director plans at year-end 2023.

nodes.title: Note 23 - Earnings per share
nodes.summary: Note 23 explains JPMorgan Chase’s EPS methods: basic EPS uses the two-class method, allocating earnings between common stock and participating unvested RSUs that receive nonforfeitable dividends; participating securities are excluded from diluted shares. Diluted EPS considers contingently issuable shares and uses whichever of the two-class or treasury stock methods is more dilutive; the two-class method prevailed in 2021–2023. The table reports the basic and diluted EPS calculations for those years, including net income allocations, weighted-average shares, dilutive awards, and per-share results.

nodes.title: Note 24 - Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.summary: Note 24 describes AOCI components: after-tax unrealized investment-security gains/losses, currency translation and related hedges, fair value and cash flow hedges, defined-benefit pension and OPEB plans, and own-credit changes on fair-value-option liabilities. It reports component balances and annual changes through 2023, plus pre-tax, tax-effect, and after-tax OCI changes for 2021–2023. Notes explain transferred securities, income-statement reclassifications, excluded cross-currency basis spreads, and the 2022 pension-settlement remeasurement.

nodes.title: Note 25 - Income taxes
Effective tax rate and expense
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase files a consolidated U.S. federal return and uses the asset-and-liability method to recognize current and deferred taxes, with valuation allowances for deferred tax assets. Tax estimates involve judgment across jurisdictions and may change as audits are resolved. The note reconciles statutory and effective tax rates for 2021–2023, reports current and deferred tax expense by jurisdiction and audit-resolution effects, explains tax items recorded in equity, presents U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income, and states that tax on global intangible low-tax income is recognized when incurred.

nodes.title: Results from Non-U.S. earnings
key_items: Note 25 – Income taxes; Effective tax rate and expense
Tax effect of items recorded in stockholders’ equity
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase files a consolidated U.S. federal return and uses the asset-and-liability method to recognize current and deferred taxes, with valuation allowances for deferred tax assets it does not expect to realize. Tax estimates require judgment across many jurisdictions and may change as audits and agreements are finalized. The note reconciles statutory and effective tax rates for 2021–2023, reports current and deferred tax expense by jurisdiction and audit-resolution effects, explains tax effects recorded in equity, presents U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income, and states that tax on global intangible low-tax income is recognized when incurred.

nodes.title: Affordable housing tax credits
nodes.summary: The Firm recognized affordable-housing investment tax credits and other tax benefits of $2.0 billion in 2023, $1.8 billion in 2022, and $1.7 billion in 2021; related amortization in income tax expense was $1.6 billion, $1.4 billion, and $1.3 billion, respectively. Investment carrying values in other assets were $14.6 billion at December 31, 2023, and $12.1 billion in 2022; related commitments in accounts payable and other liabilities were $6.8 billion and $5.4 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Deferred taxes
nodes.summary: The text explains deferred tax accounting, including recognition of deferred tax assets when realization is more likely than not and valuation allowances for assets deemed unrealizable. It presents 2023 and 2022 deferred tax asset and liability components, totals, and net deferred tax assets, and notes that net assets appear in other assets. It describes a First Republic acquisition-related deferred tax asset estimate and possible measurement-period changes. It also details tax carryforward balances, expiration periods, unlimited carryforward availability, and the reasons for the 2023 valuation allowance.

nodes.title: Unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reported unrecognized tax benefits, excluding interest and penalties, of $5.4 billion, $5.0 billion and $4.6 billion at year-end 2023, 2022 and 2021; amounts that would reduce the effective tax rate if recognized were $3.9 billion, $3.8 billion and $3.4 billion. Some benefits would not affect the rate because of temporary differences or offsets. The firm assesses these balances based on expected tax filings and ongoing audits, and estimates they could change by up to $1.1 billion over the next 12 months, resulting in a payment or income-statement impact. A reconciliation details annual additions, reductions and settlements. After-tax interest and penalties recognized in tax expense were $229 million, $141 million and $174 million for 2023–2021; accrued tax-related interest and penalties were $1.6 billion at year-end 2023 and $1.3 billion at year-end 2022.

nodes.title: Tax examination status
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reports ongoing tax examinations by U.S. and foreign authorities, listing examination periods and statuses for U.S., New York State, New York City, and U.K. entities. It describes regulatory restrictions on cash and assets, with restricted cash of $19.6 billion in 2023 versus $26.8 billion in 2022, plus customer-related restricted assets. It also explains legal limits on affiliate lending and covered transactions, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company and IHC, dividend controls and capital/liquidity restrictions, and approximately $20 billion of bank-subsidiary dividend capacity without prior regulatory approval at January 1, 2024.

The note covers JPMorgan Chase’s tax accounting methods, judgment and audit uncertainties, statutory-to-effective rate reconciliation, tax expense by jurisdiction, equity tax effects, pretax income by region, and global intangible low-tax income. It reports affordable-housing credits, amortization, investments and commitments; deferred tax assets and liabilities, carryforwards, valuation allowances and acquisition-related estimates; unrecognized tax benefits, interest, penalties and possible changes; and tax examinations. It also describes restricted assets, affiliate-transaction limits, Parent Company and IHC funding, dividend controls, and bank-subsidiary dividend capacity.

nodes.title: Note 26 - Restrictions on cash and intercompany funds transfers
key_items: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
nodes.summary: Note 26 describes regulatory restrictions on the Firm’s cash and assets, including broker-dealer restrictions and required central-bank reserves. Restricted cash totaled $19.6 billion in 2023 versus $26.8 billion in 2022; other restricted assets included customer-related pledged cash and securities ($40.5 billion versus $42.4 billion) and restricted securities ($20.5 billion versus $31.7 billion). It also explains legal limits on intercompany lending and covered transactions, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company, JPMorgan Chase Bank and the IHC, restrictions on dividends and credit, and approximately $20 billion in dividends banking subsidiaries could pay without prior regulatory approval at January 1, 2024.

nodes.title: Note 27 - Regulatory capital
nodes.summary: Federal Reserve and OCC rules set Basel III capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., assessed under the lower of Standardized or Advanced risk-based approaches. The note lists 2023 and 2022 risk-based and leverage-based minimum and well-capitalized thresholds, including buffers, surcharges, and regulatory definitions. It describes the phaseout of CECL transition benefits and reports both entities’ 2023 and 2022 capital amounts, ratios, risk-weighted assets, adjusted average assets, leverage exposure, and leverage ratios, noting both were well-capitalized and met applicable requirements.

nodes.title: Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its off-balance-sheet lending commitments, guarantees and other commitments: contractual amounts are maximum potential credit exposure but do not represent expected exposure or funding needs, as most instruments expire, are renewed, cancelled or go undrawn without default. The Firm maintains an allowance for expected losses on wholesale and certain consumer commitments (see Note 13). The table covers contractual amounts and carrying values at year-end 2023 and 2022; card and home-equity figures are total available credit, not expected simultaneous usage. The Firm may reduce or cancel card lines, typically closing them when borrowers are at least 60 days past due, and may reduce or close HELOCs after significant property-value declines or demonstrable deterioration in borrower creditworthiness.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 and 2022 off-balance-sheet lending-related instruments, guarantees, and commitments by remaining maturity and carrying value, with definitions and notes on categories, risk participations, collateral, accounting, and First Republic adjustments. Explains the nature of unfunded credit commitments and U.S. GAAP guarantee recognition, including contingent obligations and indemnifications. Details standby letters of credit, financial guarantees, and other letters of credit, including contractual amounts by internal credit rating, allowances, guarantee liabilities, carrying values, and collateralized commitments.

nodes.title: Credit Commitments and Guarantees
key_items: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
nodes.summary: Unfunded credit commitments support working capital, corporate purposes, commercial paper and bond financing, clearing organizations, and multipurpose facilities that may include standby letters of credit. The text explains U.S. GAAP guarantee definitions and accounting: initial fair-value liability recognition, subsequent premium amortization, separate recognition of lending-related expected credit losses, and recognition and treatment of probable, estimable non-lending obligations such as indemnifications. Contractual amounts and carrying values are reported in a referenced table. Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees are conditional lending commitments backing clients’ performance in financing and trade arrangements.

nodes.title: Standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and other letters of credit
key_items: Securities lending indemnifications; Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 and 2022 standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees, and other letters of credit, including contractual amounts, carrying values, related allowances and guarantee liabilities, collateralized commitments, and internal risk-rating categories. It explains securities-lending indemnities, overcollateralization, daily collateral monitoring, and cash-collateral investment indemnities. It describes derivative guarantees, including written puts and stable value contracts, their terms, exposure and fair-value measurement, and risk mitigation. A table gives 2023 and 2022 derivative guarantee notionals, limited stable-value exposures, and payables; credit protection activity is also noted, with a reference to Note 5.

nodes.title: Unsettled securities financing agreements
nodes.summary: The Firm enters into resale and securities-borrowed agreements, which at settlement involve advancing cash and receiving securities collateral, as well as repurchase and securities-loaned agreements, which involve receiving cash and providing collateral. These commitments settle at a future date, generally on regular-way terms, are usually not derivatives, and are not recorded on the Consolidated balance sheets until settlement. See Note 11 for further discussion.

nodes.title: Loan sales- and securitization-related indemnifications
key_items: Mortgage repurchase liability; Private label securitizations
nodes.summary: The Firm may have to repurchase U.S. GSE mortgage loans or indemnify purchasers if loan representations and warranties are breached; private-label securitization repurchase demands are assessed separately in litigation reserves (see Note 30). Mortgage servicing may be recourse or nonrecourse: nonrecourse credit exposure is mainly temporary servicing advances, while recourse servicing shares credit losses with loan owners when foreclosure proceeds fall short of balances, interest, and property costs. Most Firm securitizations are nonrecourse, transferring future credit risk to securities purchasers. The unpaid principal balance of recourse loans and the related recorded liability are disclosed on page 292.

nodes.title: Other off-balance sheet arrangements
key_items: Exchange & Clearing House Memberships; Sponsored member repo program
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet arrangements: tax-related and software/business-sale indemnities, whose potential exposure is difficult to estimate but loss is expected to be remote; merchant charge-backs, mitigated with reserves, collateral and valuation allowances, alongside annual processed volumes for 2021–2023; clearing-member client credit risk, margin practices, close-outs and accounting treatment; exchange and clearing-house default and investment-loss obligations; guarantees under the sponsored-member repo program, secured by collateral; and Parent Company guarantees of subsidiary obligations and debt, including fully guaranteed JPMFC securities. Management generally considers loss risk remote, with certain estimated exposures disclosed elsewhere.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet commitments, guarantees and arrangements for 2023 and 2022, including contractual amounts, carrying values, maturities, credit ratings, collateral and expected-loss allowances. Explains how commitments may expire, go undrawn or be reduced, and the accounting for credit commitments and guarantees. Covers standby letters and other guarantees, securities-lending and derivative indemnities, unsettled securities-financing transactions, loan-sale and securitization indemnifications, and other arrangements involving tax and business-sale indemnities, merchant charge-backs, clearing and exchange risks, sponsored-member repos, and Parent Company guarantees.

nodes.title: Note 29 - Pledged assets and collateral
nodes.summary: The Firm pledges owned financial assets to support borrowing capacity at Federal Reserve banks, other central banks and FHLBs, and to secure financing agreements, short sales, derivatives and deposits; secured parties may use some assets. Total pledged assets were $1,064.8 billion in 2023 versus $793.2 billion in 2022, including assets usable by secured parties ($145.0 billion and $110.8 billion), assets not so usable ($244.2 billion and $114.8 billion), and assets pledged at Federal Reserve banks and FHLBs ($675.6 billion and $567.6 billion). The 2023 amount includes $88.4 billion pledged to the FDIC for the First Republic acquisition. Totals exclude consolidated VIE assets. Pledged assets comprised investment securities, loans, and trading assets and other: $108.6 billion, $681.7 billion, and $274.5 billion in 2023; $104.4 billion, $485.9 billion, and $202.9 billion in 2022. The Firm also accepts financial collateral, mainly through resale and securities financing agreements, customer receivables, and derivatives, and uses it for financing, short sales, derivatives, and deposits. Fair value of collateral permitted to be used was $1,303.9 billion in 2023 and $1,346.9 billion in 2022; amounts actually sold, repledged, delivered, or otherwise used were $982.8 billion and $1,019.4 billion.

nodes.title: Note 30 - Litigation
Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: The Firm reports numerous legal proceedings across businesses and jurisdictions, including litigation, investigations, and regulatory actions. It estimates reasonably possible losses beyond reserves at $0–$1.3 billion, while noting substantial uncertainty and that some matters cannot be estimated. Material matters include 1MDB civil and Swiss criminal proceedings; India’s Amrapali investigation and appeal of a $31.5 million fine; remaining FX inquiries and civil suits; Zelle inquiries; interchange-fee antitrust litigation and settlements; the approved $290 million Epstein survivor settlement; LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations and litigation, including an annulled and reimposed EURIBOR fine; and Russian claims over payments restricted by sanctions, including a February 2024 judgment against the Firm.

nodes.title: Regulatory Inquiries and Litigation
key_items: Government Inquiries Related to the Zelle Network
LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: The page covers FX matters, including a pending South African inquiry and civil cases in the U.S. and abroad, with some settlements and appeals. It describes government inquiries into Zelle transfer disputes; interchange-fee litigation, including an approved $6.2 billion damages settlement, ongoing injunctive claims, and merchant settlements; the approved $290 million Epstein survivors’ settlement; and LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations and litigation, including a reimposed European fine, ongoing U.S. dollar LIBOR cases and appeals, and resolution of non-U.S. dollar LIBOR actions.

nodes.title: Russian Litigation
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase legal matters and regulatory inquiries: Russian claims seek sanctions-prohibited payments, including one judgment, and Russian-held assets could be seized; SEC inquiries concern advisory-program practices and liquidation timing, with cooperation ongoing. Securities-lending antitrust claims are preliminarily settled pending court approval. Shareholder class and derivative suits concern historical trading, fiduciary conduct, Epstein’s retention, and records preservation, with several dismissed and others pending or appealed. Trading-venue data gaps prompted remediation and review; the Firm expects two regulatory resolutions involving an independent consultant and about $350 million in penalties, is negotiating with a third regulator, and anticipates no client-service disruption.

nodes.title: Regulatory Inquiries and Litigation
nodes.summary: The Firm notes potential Russian asset seizure risk if claims there are enforced. It is cooperating with the SEC on advisory-program billing and manager selection, and liquidation timing for shares distributed to investment vehicles. A securities-lending antitrust class action alleging efforts to block anonymous exchange trading has a preliminarily approved settlement awaiting final approval. Shareholder class and derivative suits concern historical precious-metals and Treasury trading, related regulatory resolutions, Epstein’s banking relationship, and compliance-record preservation. Outcomes include dismissals, a pending appeal and motion to dismiss, and a dismissed amended class complaint.

nodes.title: Trading Venues Investigations
nodes.summary: The Firm identified gaps in CIB trading and order data flowing to surveillance systems, completed venue-inventory and data-completeness enhancements, and is nearing completion of a review that found no employee misconduct or client or market harm; one venue’s largely sponsored-client activity gap was significant. It expects resolutions with two U.S. regulators requiring remediation, an independent consultant, and about $350 million in penalties, and is negotiating with a third; client services are not expected to be disrupted. Separately, the Firm faces many legal proceedings, intends to defend them, and records and reviews reserves quarterly under U.S. GAAP. Legal expenses were $1.4 billion in 2023, $266 million in 2022, and $426 million in 2021. Outcomes and losses are uncertain; the Firm believes other pending cases will not materially affect consolidated financial condition, but losses could exceed reserves, damage reputation, or materially affect a period’s results.

The note reviews litigation, investigations and regulatory actions across jurisdictions, estimating reasonably possible losses beyond reserves at $0–$1.3 billion while noting uncertainty and unestimable matters. Topics include 1MDB, Amrapali, foreign exchange, Zelle, interchange fees, Epstein, LIBOR/EURIBOR, Russian claims and potential asset seizures; SEC inquiries; securities-lending antitrust and shareholder suits; and trading-surveillance data gaps, remediation, anticipated regulatory resolutions and penalties. It also discusses legal reserves, expenses, defenses and potential financial, reputational and period-specific impacts.

nodes.title: Note 31 - International operations
nodes.summary: Note 31 reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2021–2023 revenue, expenses, income before tax, net income, and total assets across Europe/Middle East/Africa, Asia-Pacific, Latin America/Caribbean, total international, and North America. International activity is defined by client and relationship, booking, or trading-desk location; integrated operations require estimates to allocate results, consistent with segment reporting. Long-lived assets are not significant, and most are in the U.S. North America substantially reflects the U.S.; 2023 North America includes First Republic. Revenue comprises net interest and noninterest revenue; expense includes noninterest expense and credit-loss provision. U.K. assets are also disclosed for each year.

nodes.title: Note 32 - Business segments
key_items: Consumer & Community Banking; Corporate & Investment Bank; Commercial Banking; Asset & Wealth Management
nodes.summary: Note 32 describes JPMorgan Chase’s four reportable business segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus Corporate, outlining their clients, products, organization, and functions. It explains managed-basis/FTE reporting, capital allocation and performance measures, and presents 2021–2023 segment results, reconciliations, footnotes, and the planned 2024 reorganization. Note 33 presents Parent Company-only income and comprehensive income statements, balance sheets, and cash flows for 2021–2023, with notes on intercompany interest, debt maturities, guarantees, and cash taxes.

nodes.title: Note 33 - Parent company
nodes.summary: Note 33 presents JPMorgan Chase’s Parent Company-only income and comprehensive income statements for 2021–2023, balance sheets for 2022–2023, and cash flow statements for 2021–2023, including subsidiary income, expenses, assets, liabilities, equity, operating/investing/financing cash flows, and cash balances. Footnotes explain intercompany derivative-hedge interest, scheduled long-term debt maturities, guarantees of subsidiaries’ obligations, and cash income taxes paid, including subsidiary reimbursements.

nodes.title: Note 34 - Business combinations
Note 34 - Business combinations (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s May 1, 2023 acquisition of selected First Republic assets and liabilities from the FDIC was accounted for as a U.S. GAAP business combination using estimated acquisition-date fair values. The estimated after-tax bargain gain rose from $2.7 billion to $2.8 billion after $63 million of adjustments; settlement and valuation estimates may be finalized within a year. The note describes shared-loss agreements covering 80% of specified credit losses, a $50 billion secured, five-year 3.4% Purchase Money Note, and settlement of the Firm’s earlier $5 billion deposit and related transactions. It presents the purchase-price allocation, acquired assets and assumed liabilities, related reclassifications and noncash transactions, and directs readers to other notes for accounting policies and valuation methods.

nodes.title: Core deposit and customer relationship intangibles
nodes.summary: The First Republic acquisition included a $1.3 billion core deposit intangible, valued by discounting after-tax funding-cost savings using the favorable source of funds method, and $180 million in customer relationship intangibles, valued by discounting after-tax earnings using the multi-period excess earnings method. Both valuations used market-participant assumptions, including growth and attrition, fee income, servicing costs, and discount rates. Both assets will be amortized over approximately seven years; see Note 15 for other intangible assets.

nodes.title: Indemnification assets - Shared-loss agreements
nodes.summary: The text explains First Republic acquisition accounting: FDIC shared-loss indemnification assets are initially fair-valued and subsequently remeasured through other income, with possible termination payments recorded as contingent consideration. It describes fair-value methods and balance-sheet classification for the Purchase Money Note and assumed FHLB advances. A table gives acquired loans’ May 1, 2023 unpaid principal balances and fair values, including a fourth-quarter reclassification adjustment. It reports First Republic’s 2023 contributions and unaudited 2022–2023 pro forma results, assumptions and adjustments, and cautions that expected synergies are excluded and pro forma results are not predictive.

nodes.title: Acquired Assets, Debt and Loans

nodes.title: Outstanding Preferred Stock and Ranking

nodes.title: Dividend Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock dividends are cash, noncumulative, and payable only when declared, to record-date holders, at specified rates and dates. Missed dividends are forfeited. Payment restrictions require full dividends before equal- or junior-ranking preferred dividends; partial parity payments are allocated pro rata using current amounts due for noncumulative shares and current plus accumulated unpaid amounts for cumulative shares. Until Listed Preferred dividends are fully paid or funded, junior distributions and certain junior or equal-ranking share repurchases are restricted, subject to listed exceptions for conversions, reclassifications, contemporaneous sales, pro rata offers, prior ordinary-course contracts, and incentive plans; ordinary-course market transactions remain permitted. Otherwise, junior or parity dividends may be paid from legally available assets, without participation by Listed Preferred holders. The text defines junior, parity, and senior ranking and explains dividend calculations, including annualization, 30/360 and actual-day conventions, and rounding to the nearest cent.

nodes.title: Rights Upon Liquidation
nodes.summary: Upon liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, each Listed Preferred Stock series receives $10,000 per share plus declared, unpaid dividends before junior equity; undeclared dividends do not accumulate, and holders have no claim to remaining assets after full payment. If funds are insufficient, equal-ranking series share assets proportionally. Asset sales, mergers, and consolidations do not constitute liquidation. As a holding company, subsidiary creditors may have priority over claims to subsidiary assets. Preferred holders rank behind the company’s debt and other non-equity claims and may be fully subordinated to U.S. government interests in insolvency proceedings.

nodes.title: Alerian ETN Index, Denominations, and Coupons
key_items: Coupon Payments and the Accrued Tracking Fee
nodes.summary: Alerian ETNs are unsecured, uninsured securities; “holders” refers to registered owners, and capitalized terms are defined elsewhere. Returns track an energy MLP index calculated by S&P Dow Jones Indices with its sponsor using float-adjusted market capitalization. Notes are denominated in U.S. dollars with a $19.03661 minimum principal amount. Quarterly cash coupons equal reference distributions minus an accrued fee of 0.85% annually on Daily Note Value. If distributions do not cover fees, no coupon is paid and the shortfall carries forward. Payments are quarterly in arrears, with the final coupon included in cash settlement; interim coupon amounts are calculated and published daily, while actual coupons are determined quarterly.

nodes.title: Alerian ETN Repurchase, Maturity, and Calculation Agents
nodes.summary: Repurchase notices and confirmations must meet stated deadlines, which may vary by brokerage; late or invalid submissions are ineffective, and valid notices are irrevocable. The Note Calculation Agent resolves notice and delivery questions. At maturity, unless previously repurchased, each ETN pays its Cash Settlement Amount, floored at zero, based on index returns, any final coupon and qualifying distributions, less accrued tracking fees. VWAP levels use specified multi-day averages; tracking fees and weak index performance may cause partial or total principal loss. JPMS handles ETN calculations except VWAP determinations, which an affiliated JPMorgan research group makes on non-disrupted days.

nodes.title: Market Disruption Events
nodes.summary: The text defines Averaging Dates, Disrupted Days, Market Disruption Events, and Scheduled Closing Time. A disrupted component’s VWAP and share weighting are deferred to its first succeeding non-disrupted Index Business Day, with that data applied to relevant VWAP Level calculations for both the disruption date and the scheduled averaging date. The final Averaging Date cannot be delayed more than three Index Business Days; if that day is not a business day or is disrupted, the calculation agent makes a good-faith estimate. Disruptions include exchange closures, trading suspensions or limits, impaired market access, unscheduled early closes, or events materially hindering hedge adjustment or unwinding, as determined by the agent. Announced changes to regular trading hours are excluded; certain volatility-related trading restrictions count as suspensions.

nodes.title: Discontinuation of the Index; Alteration of Method of Calculation
nodes.summary: If the Index or its data becomes unavailable, the Note Calculation Agent may select a comparable successor index, calculate VWAP from its weighted component VWAPs, or use pre-discontinuation component data with corporate-action adjustments; it must notify the Trustee, issuer, and ETN holders. Material index methodology changes trigger good-faith adjustments to preserve comparability, though discontinuation may harm ETN value. Upon continuing default and acceleration, the amount due is a cash Repurchase Amount calculated over an accelerated measurement period with no fee, with notice to the Trustee and DTC within two Business Days. The ETNs are listed on NYSE Arca as AMJ, with no assurance of continued listing or liquidity; they are DTC book-entry global notes registered to Cede & Co., with definitive notes available only in limited cases. Bank of New York Mellon or an affiliate serves as registrar and transfer agent, and the bank serves as paying agent.

nodes.title: Reissuances or Reopening Issuances
nodes.summary: The issuer may, at its sole discretion and depending on market conditions and VWAP Levels, reopen or reissue the Alerian ETNs. Additional issuances will be consolidated with the original ETNs as a single sub-series, share the same CUSIP, and trade interchangeably after settlement, increasing the aggregate outstanding principal amount. The price of each additional offering will be set when that offering is priced.

nodes.title: General Terms of the Series E Notes
nodes.summary: The section outlines general terms for JPMorgan Chase Series E Notes, including Alerian ETNs, and summarizes material provisions of the 2001 Indenture while directing investors to that document for complete terms and definitions. The notes are direct, unsecured, unsubordinated obligations ranking equally with the company’s other such debt. Because JPMorgan Chase is a holding company, noteholders generally rank behind subsidiary creditors, whose claims include debt, deposits, repurchase agreements, commercial paper, and other borrowings, except where JPMorgan Chase is recognized and paid as a subsidiary creditor.

nodes.title: Events of Default and Waivers
nodes.summary: The 2001 Indenture defines defaults as specified payment failures, uncured covenant breaches after notice, insolvency events, or defaults in supplemental terms. Continuing defaults may allow the Trustee or holders of at least 25% of the relevant securities to accelerate payment; subject to conditions, a majority may rescind acceleration or waive past defaults. Defaults may affect only one series. The Trustee generally must notify holders within 90 days, with limited exceptions, and cannot withhold notice of payment defaults. Majority holders may direct remedies, subject to Trustee protections and indemnity; individual suits require specified notice, request, delay, indemnity, and no conflicting direction. Individual payment and enforcement rights remain protected. The issuer must annually report its knowledge of defaults to the Trustee.

nodes.title: Covenant Breach
nodes.summary: The text explains that a continuing nonpayment covenant breach under the 2001 Indenture requires written notice and 90 days to cure, but does not permit acceleration; the Trustee may pursue judicial remedies for breaches or defaults. Indenture amendments generally require majority approval of each affected series, while specified material changes require every affected holder’s consent; limited corrective or non-adverse amendments need no holder consent. Mergers, consolidations, or substantially-all-asset transfers must meet successor-assumption and no-default conditions. The indenture offers no special protection for recapitalizations, change-of-control, or leveraged transactions unless structured as covered mergers or asset transfers, though issue-specific protections may be added. nodes.summary: Holders may request weekly repurchase of at least 50,000 2044 Alerian ETNs, subject to procedures and no notice to redeem all outstanding notes; the issuer may consistently lower the minimum but need not. Payment per note is closing intrinsic value over the measurement period, less a 0.125% fee (excluding unpaid coupons), floored at zero. Valuation is generally each Friday; payment follows the measurement period by the standard settlement cycle (currently two business days, expected one from May 28, 2024), capped at five. Requests require an issuer-form notice emailed by 4 p.m. ET the prior business day, a DVP trade, and DTC delivery by 10 a.m. ET on the repurchase date. Broker deadlines may vary. Notices are irrevocable, must arrive on time and be acknowledged that day; the calculation agent decides validity and receipt timing.

nodes.title: Split or Reverse Split of the 2044 Alerian ETNs
nodes.summary: The Issuer may split or reverse split the 2044 Alerian ETNs at its discretion, setting the ratio based on market indicators and giving holders notice and a press release at least three Business Days before the effective date; the record date is the preceding Business Day. It may adjust related amounts, fees, distributions, reference shares, and repurchase minimums, including retroactive adjustments to unpaid coupons. A 4-for-1 split quadruples ETNs held and generally quarters applicable values while quadrupling the repurchase minimum. In a reverse split, fractional ETNs may be compensated at the Note Calculation Agent’s discretion; the Issuer currently intends cash compensation based on a proportionate Closing Intrinsic Note Value, potentially using five-day average VWAP, determined within 20 Index Business Days of announcement and paid within five Business Days thereafter.

nodes.title: Postponement of a Payment Date
nodes.summary: Coupon Payment Dates and the Maturity Date are “Payment Dates.” A Payment Date that falls on a non-Business Day moves to the next Business Day. If a market disruption or other event postpones an Averaging Date to fewer than three Business Days before a scheduled Payment Date, that Payment Date moves to the third Business Day after the latest postponed Averaging Date. Payments are made on the adjusted date with the same effect as originally scheduled, and no interest accrues or is payable for the delay.

nodes.title: Postponement of an Averaging Date
nodes.summary: The final VWAP Level is the arithmetic average across five Averaging Dates, using component VWAPs and units and the Index Divisor. If a component is unavailable on an Averaging Date, its calculation and subsequent dates’ calculations are postponed to prevent reusing the same day’s data; no postponement extends beyond the third Index Business Day after the originally scheduled date (the Final Disrupted Averaging Date). The VWAP Calculation Agent calculates an Adjusted VWAP Level using scheduled-date data for available components and the first subsequent available-day data for unavailable components; if none becomes available by the final date, it makes good-faith estimates of market value, units, and divisor. Unavailable Days include component Disrupted Days and Prior Valuation Dates. A Disrupted Day involves an exchange closure or continuing Market Disruption Event that the Note Calculation Agent determines materially affects the VWAP Level; a Prior Valuation Date is one whose data was already used for an earlier adjusted level in the same Measurement Period.

nodes.title: Market Disruption Events
nodes.summary: A Market Disruption Event occurs when trading in an Index Component or related futures/options is suspended, absent, or limited; an event impairs participants’ ability to transact or obtain market values; or an exchange closes early without timely advance notice. The Note Calculation Agent determines events in its sole discretion, and the disruption must materially interfere with the Issuer’s or an affiliate’s ability to adjust or unwind a material hedge in the 2044 Alerian ETNs. Announced changes to regular exchange hours do not qualify; trading restrictions under rules comparable to NYSE Rule 80B during significant market fluctuations do. Scheduled Closing Time means the regular-session weekday close, excluding after-hours trading.

nodes.title: Discontinuation of the Index; Alteration of Method of Calculation
nodes.summary: If the Index is discontinued or required data become unavailable, the Note Calculation Agent may select a comparable successor index and apply a fixed adjustment to preserve comparability; written notice goes to the Trustee, Issuer and DTC. During a continuing default, accelerated payment is calculated as maturity value using a five-Index-Business-Day measurement period, with no further accrual; payment notice is due within two Business Days. The ETNs trade on NYSE Arca as AMJB, without assurance of continued listing or liquidity. They are issued as DTC-held book-entry global master notes, with beneficial interests tracked through participants; “holders” means registered owners.

nodes.title: Denominations
nodes.summary: Book-entry 2044 Alerian ETNs are issued in minimum denominations equal to the Principal Amount and whole-number multiples. The Bank of New York Mellon’s New York City principal corporate trust office handles maturity payments and transfer registration. The bank or an affiliate serves as registrar and transfer agent; the bank also acts as paying agent and may appoint additional agents. Transfers are registered without charge, subject to payment of applicable taxes or governmental charges and any required indemnity.

nodes.title: Reopening Issuances
nodes.summary: The Issuer may, but need not, issue additional 2044 Alerian ETNs without notice or consent; new notes join the same interchangeable class. Issuance restrictions, suspensions, or resumptions may affect liquidity, trading prices, premiums, and outstanding amounts, while the Issuer need not consider holders’ interests and may incur other debt or issue securities. The text then introduces the Series A Notes and summarizes Callable Notes due June 10, 2032: their governing indenture, unsecured and unsubordinated status, JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unconditional guarantee, credit risks, lack of deposit insurance, and holder-registration definition. At December 31, 2023, $5 million was outstanding. Issued June 10, 2021, in $1,000 denominations, they mature June 10, 2032, pay 2.60% interest semiannually, and may be redeemed in whole on June 10, 2031, at par plus accrued interest.

nodes.title: Key Terms of the Callable Notes
nodes.summary: The Callable Notes were issued June 10, 2021, in $1,000 denominations, mature June 10, 2032, and pay 2.60% annual interest semiannually. The issuer may redeem all, but not some, on June 10, 2031, at principal plus accrued interest, with DTC notice 5–15 business days beforehand. JPMS is calculation agent. On default acceleration, payment is $1,000 per $1,000 plus accrued interest, calculated using specified day-count and rate rules; notice of the amount is due to the trustee and DTC within two business days. The notes trade on the NYSE as JPM/32, though continued listing and liquidity are not assured. They are DTC book-entry global securities, with definitive notes available only in limited circumstances. Bank of New York Mellon serves as registrar, transfer agent, and paying agent. The issuer may reopen the notes, with additional notes sharing their CUSIP and trading interchangeably. The text also introduces general Series A debt-security terms, summarizes the 2016 Indenture while directing investors to it for full terms, and states that the notes are unsecured, unsubordinated issuer obligations fully and unconditionally guaranteed by the guarantor.

The notes trade on the NYSE as JPM/32, with no assurance of continued listing or liquidity. They are issued in DTC book-entry form, with limited exceptions for definitive notes; Bank of New York Mellon serves as registrar, transfer agent, and paying agent. The Issuer may reopen the notes, consolidating additional notes under the same CUSIP for interchangeable trading, at a price set when offered.

nodes.summary: The section outlines general terms for Series A Notes, including Callable Notes and 2044 Alerian ETNs, summarizing the 2016 Indenture while directing investors to it for complete terms and definitions. The notes are the issuer’s direct, unsecured, unsubordinated obligations, fully and unconditionally guaranteed by the Guarantor. Because the Guarantor is a holding company, noteholders’ guarantee claims generally rank behind subsidiary creditors. Proceeds-contribution requirements and limits on subsidiary payments make the Guarantor dependent on dividends and credit from subsidiaries, potentially constraining its ability to pay interest, redeem or repurchase securities, and meet other obligations.

nodes.title: Events of Default and Waivers
nodes.summary: The text defines series-specific Events of Default, including payment failures, uncured covenant breaches, Issuer insolvency, specified guarantee failures, and supplemental-indenture events, with limits for Guarantor insolvency and nonpayment covenant breaches. It explains acceleration, automatic acceleration for Issuer insolvency, and majority-holder waiver or annulment; defaults need not cross between series. It covers Trustee default notices and permissible withholding, holder directions and indemnity, conditions for individual suits, protected payment rights, annual default statements, and possible Trustee conflicts arising from banking relationships and resulting resignation and successor appointment.

nodes.title: Modification of the 2016 Indenture
nodes.summary: The 2016 Indenture generally permits amendments with majority approval from each affected series, but requires each affected holder’s consent for changes to core payment terms, currency, payment calculations, redemption amounts, enforcement or repurchase rights, voting thresholds, or adversely affected guarantees. Certain administrative or non-adverse amendments may be made without holder consent. Issuer and Guarantor mergers or asset transfers require qualifying U.S. successors to assume their respective obligations and no continuing or resulting default; specified Guarantor insolvency-related asset transfers count as transfers of substantially all assets. The Indenture offers no extra protection for recapitalizations, control changes, or leveraged transactions unless structured as covered mergers or asset transfers, though security-specific protections may be offered. The Guarantor guarantees payment fully, unconditionally, and on demand, subject to limits on amounts owed and defenses available to the Issuer (excluding insolvency-related defenses).

No added protection applies to recapitalizations, control changes, or leveraged transactions unless structured as covered mergers or asset transfers, though issue-specific protections may be offered. The award is effective on the grant date unless declined as specified, in which case it is cancelled. Each nontransferable RSU represents one common share upon vesting, supports future performance and shareholder alignment, and carries no dividend equivalents. The vesting period runs from grant to the final vesting date and may be extended or followed by share restrictions under referenced provisions.

nodes.title: Protection-Based Vesting
nodes.summary: RSUs generally vest with continued employment or qualifying exceptions, but up to 50% may be cancelled at the CEO’s discretion for sustained performance concerns, negative firm pre-tax pre-provision income, relevant Line of Business threshold failures, or a Firmwide threshold failure. Such decisions require committee ratification (and Board ratification for CEO awards); cancellation rules also apply to certain continued-vesting or government-related acceleration cases. Vested distributions, net of tax withholding, are restricted from transfer or encumbrance for 12 months, except upon death. The award is subject to the firm’s Bonus Recoupment Policy and EMEA malus/clawback policy, including reductions or recovery in specified circumstances. Employment termination generally cancels outstanding RSUs, except for death or stated qualifying cases; eligible employees may continue vesting subject to the award’s conditions. Job elimination requires HR determination, cooperation after notice, and satisfaction of release/certification requirements; Full Career Eligibility is also listed as an exception.

nodes.title: RSU Vesting, Holding and Recoupment Terms

nodes.summary: The page explains continued vesting after certain protected terminations, subject to cancellation rules and committee ratification (with Board ratification for CEO awards). Vested distributions are restricted from transfer or encumbrance for 12 months, except upon death. The award and 2023 cash incentive are subject to the Bonus Recoupment Policy; the award and 2022 cash incentive are also subject to EMEA malus and clawback rules, including for financial downturns or increased capital requirements. RSUs generally cancel upon termination, but may continue vesting under specified exceptions. Job Elimination eligibility requires an HR determination, cooperation after notice, and satisfaction of release/certification requirements.

nodes.title: Full Career Eligibility
nodes.summary: Continued award vesting after termination may be available for Full Career Eligibility, Government Office, or Disability, subject to the Firm’s discretion and specified conditions. Full Career Eligibility requires five years’ continuous service, 15 years’ recognized service or 30 years’ combined service and professional experience, 180 days’ advance written notice and cooperative service, prior approval of continued vesting, restrictions on financial-services work and working in one’s profession for 36 months (with government, education, and nonprofit exceptions), and release/certification requirements. The Firm may require services during or shorten the notice period, but not below the service threshold; other notice policies may apply. Disability requires qualifying inability to return to work, a written request within 30 days, supporting documentation, Firm consent, and release requirements. In all cases, timely execution of the Firm’s release and compliance with award terms are required; Full Career and Government Office cases also require notice of restriction breaches within 15 days or periodic certifications through vesting. Government Office terms are addressed elsewhere. The text ends with a ‘Death’ heading.

nodes.title: Continued Vesting After Employment Ends
nodes.summary: Continued vesting may be allowed for qualifying voluntary retirement after specified service, notice, performance, and 36-month work restrictions, subject to the Firm’s discretion and possible notice-period changes. Government Office departures are addressed by separate requirements. Disability-related vesting requires qualifying inability to return to work, timely written request, documentation, and Firm consent. In all cases, eligibility requires a timely release, applicable advance confirmation and written consent, ongoing compliance certification or prompt notice of noncompliance, and adherence to the Award Agreement.

nodes.title: Death
nodes.summary: If you die while eligible to vest in the award’s RSUs, they immediately vest and, after tax withholding, are distributed as Common Stock to your recorded beneficiary. If none is designated, survives you, or is locally unrecognized, shares go to your estate unless local law requires otherwise. Distribution is due by the end of the calendar year following your death; the Firm’s administrative practice is to register shares within 60 days of receiving required documentation.

nodes.title: Confidentiality & Non-Solicitation
nodes.summary: The text sets employment-period and post-employment non-solicitation restrictions covering employees, former employees, and certain customers or business contacts, with exceptions for authorized work, specified job eliminations, and publicly known institutional customers; California employees instead face a narrower restriction on using confidential information to interfere with relationships. It requires advance notice to the Firm of certain information requests and cooperation with the Firm, prohibits knowingly or recklessly false statements, requires cooperation in Firm matters (with reasonable expense reimbursement), and authorizes compliance inquiries and disclosure of award terms to affected third parties. Employees subject to notice periods must give required notice, remain loyal and work during any service period or paid leave, and receive salary and certain benefits; the parties may modify or waive notice, but a separate 180-day notice rule applies to full-career eligibility termination. Finally, up to all outstanding RSUs may be cancelled for specified detrimental conduct, risk failures, inaccurate metrics or misrepresentation, cause, breach of obligations or restrictions, missed forms, or notice/cooperation failures; the Firm may also suspend vesting or share distribution as allowed by the award.

nodes.title: Award Agreement Conduct and Notice Obligations
nodes.summary: The page prohibits knowingly or recklessly false statements about the Firm and its people, while preserving lawful reporting and cooperation with authorities. It requires cooperation in Firm investigations and proceedings, with reasonable expense reimbursement, and information needed to assess Award Agreement compliance; the Firm may disclose award terms to affected third parties. It sets advance notice, service, loyalty, and compensation requirements during applicable notice periods, permits mutual changes, and reiterates a separate 180-day notice requirement for Full Career Eligibility. A Remedies section is also included.

nodes.title: Detrimental Conduct, Risk Related and Other Cancellation/Recapture
nodes.summary: The award permits cancellation of up to 100% of outstanding RSUs for specified harmful conduct, inaccurate metrics or misrepresentation, risk-management failures, termination for Cause, breaches of termination requirements, missing forms, or violations of obligations. JPMorgan Chase may suspend vesting or distributions during review. It may recover the fair market value of previously distributed shares for qualifying misconduct or breaches within three years, or detrimental conduct within one year; notice, tax-withholding exclusions, payment in shares or cash, and the non-penalty nature of recovery are specified. These provisions do not limit other recoupment policies. The Firm may seek injunctions for violations of obligations and may satisfy withholding taxes through share retention or sales, cash withholding, or delayed release of shares.

nodes.title: Award Recovery, Injunctions, and Taxes

Recovery may require repayment of the fair market value of previously distributed shares for specified misconduct or detrimental conduct within applicable three- or one-year lookback periods. Notices, tax-withholding exclusions, payment methods, and preservation of other clawback obligations are addressed. The Firm may obtain injunctions for violations of employee obligations and may use share retention, sales, cash withholding, or delayed share release to satisfy taxes.

nodes.title: RSU Award Terms and Protections
nodes.summary: The Firm may set off award-related debts against vesting proceeds, but generally cannot take assets held under a separate account agreement without consent. RSUs confer no ownership or voting rights before issuance; shares may be placed in designated accounts, restricted, or cancelled, with potential recovery obligations. The agreement binds successors, creates no employment guarantee or future-award entitlement, and does not count toward severance. Section 409A governs distributions, including specified-employee delays. Corporate share changes trigger equitable adjustments.

nodes.title: Interpretation/Administration
nodes.summary: The Committee has broad, delegable authority to interpret and administer the award, make binding and non-uniform decisions, and resolve claims. It may amend the agreement, generally without materially harming rights absent consent, subject to stated legal, vesting, restriction, and written-signature conditions. Unenforceable terms may be reformed. Distribution may be accelerated when government ethics or conflict rules require divestment, subject to Section 409A and continued obligations and recovery rules. Acceptance authorizes personal-data processing and international transfers; withdrawing consent where legally permitted cancels the award, except for required reporting and compliance. New York law governs. Disputes may be sent to AAA arbitration at the Firm’s election; otherwise, exclusive venue is the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, with objections waived to the extent permitted.

If the Firm prevails in covered enforcement proceedings, it may recover reasonable legal fees and expenses, while recipients waive advancement and indemnification.
